Selling in Minneapolis?

Ways to sell a house fast in Minneapolis

You can list with an agent, sell on your own, or sell directly to a cash buyer. Whichever route you take, a house, duplex or townhouse in the city needs a Truth in Sale of Housing report before anyone can be shown through it, so that step shapes your schedule more than the choice of buyer does.

Minneapolis has 430,324 residents on 54 square miles of land. Owners live in 47.7 percent of homes, so plenty of houses change hands between investors, landlords and first-time buyers as well as long-term owners. The typical owner-occupied home is valued at $362,200, rent is $1,371 and owners with a mortgage pay a median $2,128 a month, across 192,734 households. The average commute is 22.0 minutes. A bungalow near a lake and a duplex on a busy corridor can sit far from those middle figures, so treat them as context and not as an appraisal.

  • Agent listing: the widest exposure, though showings wait for the city report to be filed and displayed.
  • Sale by owner: the same city report applies, and you handle disclosures and paperwork yourself.
  • Cash sale: the buyer takes the house in its present condition, and the report still has to exist for the transfer.

The Truth in Sale report before showings

The city requires a Truth in Sale of Housing (TISH) evaluation for single-family houses, duplexes, townhouses and first-time condominium conversions, and the full report must exist before you show the property. It applies to sales by owner, sales through an agent, advertising a home for sale, contracts for deed and other title transfers. The city's TISH page explains the program.

You hire an evaluator approved by Minneapolis. Evaluators are not city employees and set their own prices, so comparing quotes is reasonable. The evaluator inspects the building inside and outside, writes the disclosure report and files it online where you and the city can both see it.

A report stays valid for two years or one sale, whichever ends first. Keep a copy on display so prospective buyers can read it at showings. A separate pre-inspection report does not replace it.

Two situations skip the evaluation: a property holding a Certificate of Code Compliance (issued when a house comes out of condemnation, good for up to one year) or a Certificate of Occupancy for a newly built home (good for one sale).

If the report lists repairs

When the evaluator lists required repairs, you can complete them and receive a Certificate of Approval online, or sell with the repairs open and pass them to the buyer. If the work is still undone at closing, the buyer signs an acknowledgement of responsibility, and the city asks for that form within one business day of closing. The buyer then has 90 days after closing to finish the repairs.

Open repairs on a Minneapolis TISH report
SituationPaperworkWho finishes the work
Seller finishes all repairsCertificate of ApprovalSeller, before the sale
Repairs still open at closingBuyer's signed acknowledgementBuyer, within 90 days
Buyer later resellsNew reportBuyer, before reselling

Before you book the evaluation, review the city's list of commonly required repairs and fix what you can, since fixed items will not appear on the report. After the buyer completes the work, an evaluator or a city inspector reinspects, and a successful result brings a Certificate of Completion.

For a seller with a dated house, this is the main cost question. Minneapolis Truth in Housing is reachable at 612-673-5840.

How Hennepin County taxes affect your sale

Hennepin County collects Minneapolis property tax in two halves, due May 15 and October 15. A 15th that falls on a non-business day slides to the next business day. Statements and valuation notices arrive in March, and the valuation shows how the property was assessed as of January 2.

That timing matters when you sell. A summer sale leaves the second-half bill still ahead, and the assessment you see in March sets next year's tax. Your share depends on the assessor's value, how the property is classified and the levies of the taxing districts that cover it, and more than 70 local governments levy in the county. The county's property tax line is 612-348-3011.

Your purchase agreement decides who covers the current year's bill, so ask the title company how it will be apportioned.

Disclosure and zoning questions

Minnesota law requires a written seller disclosure before you sign a purchase agreement. Under Minnesota Statutes 513.55, you list material facts you know that could significantly affect an ordinary buyer's use and enjoyment, and the disclosure must be made in good faith. A leaking basement, a past sewer backup or an unpermitted addition belongs there.

The city's 2040 Comprehensive Plan ended single-family-only zoning citywide. A buyer evaluating your lot may ask what the zoning would allow, so ask the city's planning staff before you answer.

Seasonal timing and neighborhoods

Winter timing is real. Summers run hot and humid and winters bring heavy snow, so exterior photos, roof condition and drainage are easier to show in spring and fall. The city has 83 neighborhoods, and buyers often search by neighborhood and by distance to light rail, which the Metro Blue and Green lines provide.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Minneapolis houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

When a cash sale makes sense

A cash sale tends to suit owners facing a deadline, an inherited house, tenants who will not leave, or repairs that a TISH report would make visible. The buyer purchases the house as it stands, and the open repair items move to the new owner through the acknowledgement process.

Compare any offer to what the same house would net after listing costs, a repair list and carrying costs while it sits. Ask who pays for the evaluation, how the buyer handles the city paperwork and when funds arrive. You can also request a written offer with no obligation and a firm closing date.

Getting ready before the evaluator arrives

Clear access to the basement, attic, furnace, water heater and electrical panel, and unlock any outbuildings. Replace burned-out bulbs, fix loose handrails and test the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, since small items like these often appear on a report. Gather permits for past work and any receipts for repairs. Keep the evaluation, the disclosure and your tax statement in one folder, so you can hand each to the buyer or title company without a search. Ask the evaluator how long the filing takes so you can plan your first showing around it.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a Truth in Sale of Housing report to sell my Minneapolis house?

Yes for most houses. Single-family houses, duplexes, townhouses and first-time condominium conversions need the report before the property is shown. A Certificate of Code Compliance or a Certificate of Occupancy for a new build can replace it.

How long is a Minneapolis TISH report good for?

Two years or one sale, whichever comes first. A buyer who finishes any open repairs must obtain a new report before reselling.

Who pays for repairs listed on the city report?

The purchase agreement decides. If repairs remain open at closing, the buyer signs an acknowledgement of responsibility, files it within one business day, and finishes the work within 90 days.

What dates does Hennepin County set for Minneapolis property tax?

May 15 and October 15. When either lands on a weekend or holiday, you have until the next business day.

Can I sell a Minneapolis house that needs major repairs?

Yes. The report must still be filed and displayed, but you are allowed to sell with required repairs outstanding if the buyer accepts them and signs the acknowledgement. A cash buyer often takes that route.

Selling in St. Paul?

Before you sell a house in St. Paul

St. Paul adds a step that most Minnesota cities lack: an evaluator approved by the city must inspect most one- and two-unit homes before the listing goes live. The city calls it Truth-in-Sale of Housing, or TISH, and it applies to single-family houses, duplexes, condominiums and townhomes.

The rest of the process looks like a sale anywhere in the state. You sign a disclosure, record a deed in Ramsey County and settle taxes at closing. Your route, whether an agent listing, an owner sale or a direct cash offer, changes the timeline more than the paperwork.

St. Paul housing numbers

An estimated 306,684 people lived in St. Paul on July 1, 2025, 1.5% fewer than the 311,503 counted in April 2020. Housing figures for 2020 to 2024:

  • 125,249 households averaging 2.37 people
  • 52.9% of homes owner-occupied, so nearly half of the housing stock is rented
  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $294,500
  • Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage: $1,911
  • Median gross rent: $1,281
  • Median household income: $73,394

Many St. Paul sellers hold rental or inherited property. A house that sat as a rental for years often has deferred repairs, and the TISH report records them for buyers.

Who needs a TISH report, and when

Owners of single-family homes, duplexes, condominiums and townhomes need a TISH evaluation before the home is marketed for sale. Buildings with three or more units, commercial buildings and mixed-use buildings are outside the program. A condominium with its own Ramsey County parcel number still needs a report even when the building holds a certificate of occupancy, because that certificate only covers common areas.

The report must be available to any prospective buyer within three calendar days of listing. It stays good for 365 days and covers one sale by the owner named on it. If your offer is accepted inside that year, closing can fall after the expiration date without a new report.

The evaluator is a private contractor who holds a city license, and the evaluator sets the fee. The city doesn't recommend anyone. Call the Department of Safety and Inspections at 651-266-8989 before you list if you are unsure whether your sale needs a report.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your St. Paul house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What the TISH report requires you to fix

Very little. The report is disclosure only, and the single mandatory item in a single-family house is a working hard-wired smoke alarm. If the evaluator marks it as a hazard, the city's electrical inspector sends a letter and you must hire an electrical contractor with a license to pull a permit and install the alarm. The contractor then calls the inspector to close the permit.

Everything else on the report informs the buyer and doesn't force a repair. Sellers who want to avoid hazard marks can fix items first, and the city publishes a list of the ten most common deficiencies for that purpose. Ignoring the program is a misdemeanor under Chapter 189 of the Saint Paul Legislative Code.

TISH exemptions and special cases

Truth-in-Sale of Housing rules
TISH situationWhat applies
Covered propertiesSingle-family, duplex, condominium, townhome
Not coveredThree or more units, commercial, mixed-use
Deadline to have report on handWithin three calendar days of listing
Report validity365 consecutive days, one sale
Accepted substitutesCertificate of Code Compliance or current Certificate of Occupancy
Family exemptionGrandparents, parents, children, grandchildren, siblings
Vacant buildingsCategory 1 needs a report before sale; Categories 2 and 3 need a code compliance inspection

Aunts, uncles and cousins don't count as immediate family under the program. A smoking policy disclosure form is also required when you sell a unit in a condominium, townhome or similar community.

Rent stabilization and a rental house

St. Paul's rent stabilization ordinance matters to your buyer more than to you, but it affects what the property is worth. Rent increases are capped at 3% in a 12-month period unless an exception applies.

  • Self-certification: available for increases from 3% to 8%, evaluated each year
  • Just cause vacancy: the consumer price index change plus 8%, after city review
  • Staff determination: no fixed limit when the landlord justifies the figure
  • Separate tracks exist for new construction and for low-income housing providers

A tenant-occupied house therefore comes with limits on how fast the next owner can raise the rent. Vacant houses give a buyer more room, which is one reason investors look at emptied rentals. If tenants live in the home, ask the city's Rent Stabilization team at 651-266-8553 how the rules apply to your unit.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy St. Paul houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Neighborhoods and older houses

St. Paul covers 56.18 square miles, of which 51.98 are land, and the city planning office divides it into 17 planning districts, each with a council that weighs in on land use. Older neighborhoods near downtown and along the river carry homes from the steamboat and railroad eras. On the south side, the former Ford assembly plant site in Highland Park is being redeveloped as Highland Bridge, planned with about 3,800 housing units.

The city expects more spring and summer rain over time, which can lead to river and flash flooding. Buyers and inspectors look hard at basements, roofs and drainage for that reason, so have answers ready.

Transit, schools and campuses

Interstates 94 and 35E cross the city, along with US 52 and Minnesota 280 and 5. The METRO Green Line runs along University Avenue to Minneapolis, and Amtrak's Empire Builder stops at Union Depot. Saint Paul Public Schools is the state's largest district, and families can also use charter schools, private schools and open enrollment.

Macalester College, the University of St. Thomas, Hamline University and Saint Catherine University all sit within the city, which keeps demand steady for houses near campuses.

Closing steps for a St. Paul sale

Minnesota requires a written disclosure of material facts about the property before you sign a sale agreement, under Minnesota Statutes 513.55. The disclosure must be made in good faith and reflect what you know.

The deed gets recorded in Ramsey County, where St. Paul sits. Ask the recorder for current recording fees and ask your title company who files the paperwork. Keep your TISH report, any smoke alarm permit and repair receipts together so your closing agent can pass copies to the buyer.

A direct sale to a cash buyer changes the schedule, but the city rules above still apply to the property. Ask Safety and Inspections whether a report is needed before you accept an offer. With a cash buyer, the lender and appraisal steps drop out, so the TISH report, the disclosure and the deed become the main items on your list.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a TISH report to sell my St. Paul house?

Yes, if it is a single-family home, duplex, condominium or townhome and the sale is not to immediate family. Buildings with three or more units are exempt. The report must be on hand within three calendar days of listing.

How long is a TISH report valid?

It is valid for 365 consecutive days and covers one sale by the owner named on it. If a seller accepts an offer within that year, closing may fall afterward without a new report.

What is the one repair TISH can force?

A working hard-wired smoke alarm in single-family homes. If one is missing or not working, the city sends a letter and an electrician with a license must install one under a permit.

Does Ramsey County or the city record my deed?

Ramsey County records deeds for St. Paul property. The city handles the TISH report, rental rules and permits, so you deal with two offices during a sale.

Can I sell a house with tenants in St. Paul?

Yes. Existing leases continue under the rent stabilization rules, which cap increases at 3% a year unless an exception is granted. Call the city's Rent Stabilization team at 651-266-8553 for questions about your unit.

Selling a Rochester house: what to know first

Rochester, the Olmsted County seat, lies in the bluff country of southeast Minnesota, 85 miles from the Twin Cities. It had 124,292 residents on July 1, 2025, 2.4 percent more than in April 2020, and only two Minnesota cities are bigger. Medicine drives the economy, and workers and students keep a steady stream of renters and first-time buyers in the market.

Rochester housing at a glance (2020-2024 estimates)
Housing measureRochester figure
Households51,131
Homes lived in by their owners65.1%
Median value of an owner-occupied home$310,500
Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage$1,864
Median gross rent$1,399
Median household income$89,389

Not every owner has time for a retail listing. Typical situations in a university and hospital town include:

  • a relocation after a residency, fellowship or job change;
  • a rental left behind by a tenant who moved out;
  • a house inherited from a relative who lived far away;
  • an older home with deferred repairs that would be expensive to fix before listing.

Older houses, wind and storm damage

Rochester gets around 33 inches of rain and nearly 52 inches of snow in a typical year, and the January to April stretch is the windiest. Severe storms have left a record, including tornadoes in 1953, 1962 and June 2010 and a June 2019 storm in southwest Rochester.

  • Roof and siding that have taken years of wind are the first things an inspector looks at.
  • Basements near the Zumbro and its creeks deserve a moisture check before you list or accept an offer.
  • Frozen-pipe damage in a vacant house is a real winter risk, so keep the heat on during a sale.

Cash buyers commonly accept a storm-worn house as is, so you skip the repair bids.

Construction near the river and the medical campus can change the feel of a nearby block, and buyers near downtown will likely raise it. Rochester Public Schools divides the city into John Marshall, Mayo and Century high school zones, so ask the district which zone an address falls in before it goes into a listing.

Selling a Rochester rental house

Anyone renting out a dwelling in Rochester needs a Rental Housing Certificate under city ordinance chapter 7-3-2, including a single-family house the owner does not live in. Renting without one is a misdemeanor punishable by up to a $1,000 fine, 90 days in jail, or both.

  • Certificates renew each year, and the fee depends on the number of units.
  • Inspection scores set a one, two, three or four year cycle, and a compliant inspection is required in the year it is due.
  • A certificate must be transferred within 30 days of a property sale, and the city has a termination form for owners who have sold.
  • A building that sits vacant must be registered within 30 days under ordinance 7-14-6, and an annual vacant building fee follows.

Short stays of up to 30 days follow separate rules. A second home listed on a rental platform needs a Short Term Rental license and a compliant inspection, while an owner-occupied room rental needs registration. For questions, the Community Development office is at 4001 W. River Parkway NW, Suite 100, and the city's main line is 507-328-2311.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Rochester house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Olmsted County property taxes at closing

House tax is split into a May 15 payment and an October 15 payment, while farm parcels run later, in mid-November. The next bill for a house comes due in May.

For a sale during the year, the county prorates tax at closing. The seller owes tax from January until closing day, and the buyer owes it from closing through December 31. A seller who prepaid the entire year is repaid for the buyer's part. A buyer who closes mid-year receives no mailed statement, yet late payment is still late.

After a sale the county mails the new owner a homestead application. Return it, because the homestead classification determines the value exclusion that lowers the tax bill. Questions go to the county's revenue and records line at 507-328-7636.

How to appeal your Rochester property value

Gather recent appraisals or comparable sales and bring them to the Assessor's Office (507-328-7670, Property Records, 151 4th Street SE). Unresolved disputes go to the meetings printed on the valuation notice, local board first where one exists and the county board where it does not.

Past that, the Minnesota Tax Court takes petitions once the valuation notice has arrived, with an April 30 cutoff in the year the tax is payable. A petition can be served by email or delivered in person to the County Attorney's Office on Fourth Street Southeast. Valuation notices arrive each spring, which opens a fresh round every year.

A step-by-step order for a quick Rochester sale

Decide first whether the house is a rental, because that sets the city paperwork. If it is, check the certificate and the inspection cycle, then ask Community Development how the transfer will work. Next, test for radon or gather the results you already have, and write down what you know about the house. Collect cash offers, compare the check amount and closing date, and sign with the buyer you trust. The deed then goes to the recorder with the deed tax, and the year's property tax is prorated between you and the buyer. Hold on to your latest tax statement for the title company. Ask the buyer in writing when you must move out.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Rochester houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Deed tax and disclosure steps

The state deed tax is 0.33 percent of net consideration, with a flat $1.65 when the price is $3,000 or less (Minn. Stat. 287.21), and the recorder collects it as soon as the deed arrives. Ask Olmsted County Property Records and Licensing how it wants deeds submitted.

State law adds a radon step ahead of any signed sale agreement: the seller discloses test results and any mitigation system in writing and hands over the Department of Health booklet on radon in real estate (Minn. Stat. 144.496). Transfers to heirs are exempt.

Before you sign anything, also gather what you know about the house for the written disclosure of material facts, and settle any rental certificate questions so the closing is not delayed.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell a Rochester house without fixing it first?

Yes, if the buyer takes it as is. Material facts you know about still go to the buyer in writing (Minn. Stat. 513.55), and a landlord should settle the rental certificate and inspection status before taking an offer on an occupied rental.

Do I need to tell a buyer about radon?

Yes. Minnesota requires a written radon disclosure before you sign an agreement to sell residential property, and a seller who withholds known radon facts can be sued within two years after closing. The disclosure covers any tests, reports and mitigation system you know about.

What happens to my rental certificate when I sell a Rochester rental?

It has to be transferred within 30 days of the sale, and the city offers a termination form for owners who have sold. Contact Community Development at 507-328-2311 so the certificate does not stay in your name.

How is tax split when a Rochester house closes?

Tax from January up to closing is the seller's, and tax from closing through December 31 is the buyer's. A seller who prepaid the full year is reimbursed at closing for the buyer's share.

When can I appeal my Rochester assessment?

Each spring, once the valuation notice arrives. Start with the county meetings, and file any Minnesota Tax Court petition by April 30 of the year the tax is payable.

What a Bloomington seller must do before listing

Before you list, show or sell a house in Bloomington, the city requires a Time-of-Sale housing inspection and a filed evaluation report. The rule covers single and two-family dwellings, condominiums, townhouses and mobile homes, and it applies to private sales as well, including a sale to a family member that is never listed. Multi-family rental buildings of four or more units are left out.

The requirement shapes the whole timeline. Cash buyers purchase as-is, but the inspection step still applies to the sale. The rest of this page walks through what the inspection costs, what it can force you to fix and who can take on a hazard.

How the Time-of-Sale inspection works

The owner or listing agent schedules the inspection with the Building and Inspections Division at 952-563-8930 or through an online request form, and the evaluator needs about 120 minutes on site.

Bloomington Time-of-Sale inspection costs
ChargeAmount
Inspection, with energy disclosure and re-inspections$250
Service fee, e-check$1.95
Service fee, card2.95 percent
Refund if you cancel before a site visitUp to 50 percent, within 60 days of your request
  • The evaluator examines visible structure, heating, electrical and plumbing, and accessible attics and crawl spaces, and does not take anything apart.
  • The report does not cover lead paint, radon or asbestos, and it does not guarantee the home.
  • The report must be displayed at the house and given to the buyer before or at sale, and a copy must reach the city within 7 calendar days.
  • The report and the Certificate of Compliance are good for one year and only for the owner named on them.

Since April 2022 the inspection has included an energy disclosure covering the heating and cooling system, water heater, insulation and windows. No energy upgrades are required of the seller.

Immediate hazards and who pays to fix them

Only nine categories of defect must be corrected, and the seller is responsible unless the buyer agrees in writing to take them over. They are unsafe heating systems, unsafe water heaters, dangerous electrical conditions, unsanitary plumbing, structures unable to carry their loads, roofs, walls and foundations that are not weather tight, abandoned fuel tanks, unsanitary refuse or infestation, and missing or non-working smoke detectors.

Other defects are noted in the report but do not have to be repaired. If hazards are found, a re-inspection by a city inspector is required before the house can be occupied, and the owner or contractor must pull any permits. A buyer who is willing to take the hazards must get the city's written consent by signing a Hazard Correction/Responsibility form, which is currently handled through DocuSign by calling the same 952-563-8930 line. The Certificate of Compliance is typically required at closing.

A realistic timeline for the inspection step

Start with the call to 952-563-8930, since the evaluator needs about 120 minutes on site and the visit has to fit around your showings. Once the report is filed, display it at the house and give it to the buyer before or at sale. The city must have a copy within 7 calendar days. If the evaluator finds one of the nine hazards, the repair and the re-inspection come before the house can be occupied, so build that time into any closing date you promise.

The Certificate of Compliance is typically required at closing, and the report and certificate last one year for the named owner only. If a sale falls through and you relist within the year, the same paperwork still works. If the house changes owners or the year runs out, you start over. Sellers who plan a cash sale should still budget for the $250 charge, because the buyer buying as-is does not remove the requirement. Keep a printed copy of the report in the house for showings, and email a copy to your title company so it is in the file well before the signing date.

Which sales are exempt?

Five kinds of transfer are exempt, but you must still call the city to say which exemption you are using. They are a newly built dwelling transferred to its first owner, a multiple dwelling that already holds a rental license, a sale to a public body, a sale for demolition, and a sale by a sheriff or other court officer. The last exemption does not cover a sale by someone appointed by a probate court, which matters for heirs selling an inherited Bloomington house.

If your sale does not fit an exemption, plan for the inspection and the report date before you set a closing. Check any open work permits as well, because the owner or contractor must obtain the necessary permits and the dwelling is subject to re-inspection of open permits before occupancy.

Bloomington housing market

Bloomington has 89,034 residents, and the typical buyer is shopping a mid-priced suburb. Median home value is $361,700 for 2020 to 2024, and 65.7 percent of homes are owner-occupied. Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage is $2,052 and median gross rent is $1,561. Interstate 35W divides the city informally, and school attendance lines run near France and Xerxes Avenues in ISD 271, so a buyer will ask which side you are on.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Bloomington houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

City fees and bills to clear before closing

Call the city to find out whether anything is owed on the property, because outstanding items are easier to clear before the title company asks. These are the numbers to use:

  • Assessing Division: 952-563-8722, for fees or fines associated with the property.
  • Utility Billing: 952-563-8726, for the current outstanding water bill.
  • Environmental Health: 952-563-8934, for pending civil fines.
  • Finance: 952-563-4527, for pending weeds, trees, brush removal and abatements.

Hennepin County taxes and recording

Hennepin County bills the property tax, due May 15 and October 15. It takes recordings by appointment, online through its Virtual Recorder site with a $3 service fee, by mail or through eRecording for title companies. Recording costs $46 per document, plus a $54 well disclosure certificate when one is needed. Properties with delinquent taxes cannot be transferred under Minnesota Statute 272.12. Minnesota Statute 513.55 separately requires a written seller disclosure before the purchase agreement is signed.

Put the pieces in order: book the Time-of-Sale inspection first, since the report date and any hazard repairs set your earliest closing. Then clear city bills, then settle the tax balance, then schedule recording.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Bloomington inspection required for a cash sale?

Yes. It applies to any sale of a covered dwelling, cash or financed, listed or private. The only way out is one of the five exemptions in city code, and you still have to call the city to say which one applies.

Do I have to repair everything the Bloomington inspector finds?

No. Only the nine immediate hazard categories must be corrected, and the buyer can assume them with the city's written consent. Other deficiencies are listed in the report without a repair requirement.

How long is a Bloomington Time-of-Sale report valid?

One year from the date of issue, and only for the owner named on it.

Who gets the Certificate of Compliance?

The city sends it to the owner or listing agent once no hazards remain. It is typically required at closing, so ask your agent or title company to confirm they have it before the signing date.

Can an heir selling an inherited house in Bloomington skip the inspection?

Usually not. The sheriff and court-officer exemption does not apply to a sale by a person appointed by a probate court, so a personal representative should plan for the inspection and report.

Selling in Duluth?

Your options for selling in Duluth

You can list through an agent, sell the house yourself, or take a direct cash offer. The best route depends on repairs, timing and what the house is used for.

With average time on market at 19 days in 2024, a well-prepared Duluth listing can move quickly. A cash sale suits a vacation rental owner who cannot transfer a permit, a landlord ending a license, a house with winter damage, or an estate that needs to close without repairs. Compare any offer with the median sale price, ask for the terms in writing, and keep your tax, permit and disclosure paperwork in one folder.

Duluth at a glance

Duluth is a port city on the western tip of Lake Superior and the county seat of St. Louis County. The July 2025 population estimate is 88,330. The city climbs a steep hillside from the lakeshore to the plateau above, with neighborhoods such as Piedmont Heights and Bayview Heights sitting up top with long views. Over the hill, the Miller Hill Mall area and the big-box strips along the Miller Trunk Highway corridor form a separate retail center. Steep streets and elevation changes make the exact address matter more here than in a flat suburb.

For 2020-2024 the owner-occupied rate is 59.4 percent, the median value of owner-occupied homes is $242,700 and median gross rent is $1,087. Median household income is $68,807, and 39.4 percent of households rent. Most public school students attend Duluth Public Schools, Independent School District 709.

Prices and days on market

Single-family prices in Duluth have climbed every year since 2021, and homes sold faster in 2024 than in 2023. Use these figures to judge any offer you receive.

Duluth single-family median sale price and average days on market

In 2024 there were 1,195 single-family listings and 1,033 sales.

How does Duluth weather affect an older house?

Winters are long and the lake adds heavy snow. Snow cover usually lasts from late November to early April, and average snowfall is 90.2 inches. Lake-effect storms can leave a foot or more near the shore while places 50 miles inland get much less.

A house here carries a heavy load from snow, ice and freeze-thaw cycles, so roofs, gutters, foundations and insulation draw attention from buyers and inspectors. Keep heating and insulation records handy, clear walks and roofs during showings, and keep the driveway plowed.

Housing and building codes that touch a sale

Duluth keeps its housing rules in the city's Legislative Code, and several chapters matter at a sale.

  • Chapter 29A covers housing, property maintenance and rental licensing. The Life Safety Division of the Fire Department administers it, and it adopts the 2012 International Property Maintenance Code.
  • Chapter 30 covers abandoned property and inoperable vehicles.
  • Chapter 50, the Unified Development Code, is the zoning code.
  • Chapter 10 adopts the Minnesota building code, and the 2020 edition took effect in Duluth on March 31, 2020.

About 17,633 units held active rental licenses in 2024. Construction Services and Inspections is at 411 West First Street, Room 100, and the phone number is 218-730-5240. If the house had a fire, Duluth withholds fire escrow funds under Minnesota Statutes 65A.50, so ask the city what applies before you accept an offer.

Can a Duluth vacation rental permit transfer to a buyer?

No. Duluth requires a city permit to rent any part of a property on Airbnb, Vrbo or similar sites, and existing vacation dwelling units are not transferable to another owner. An Interim Use Permit lasts six years or until ownership changes, whichever comes first.

There are three kinds of permit. An Accessory Home Share Permit applies when the owner lives in the building and allows stays of 1 to 29 nights, with up to 4 guests in 2 bedrooms. An Accessory Vacation Dwelling Unit, Limited Permit covers an owner-occupied homestead rented for 2 to 7 nights, to a maximum of 21 nights a year. Interim Use Permits allow 2 to 29 nights, a local property manager and no more than 9 guests. Those permits are subject to a city-wide cap outside the form districts, and the waiting list is expected to take several years. A buyer who wants income from short stays should confirm eligibility with Planning at 218-730-5580 before closing.

Recording and disclosure in St. Louis County

The St. Louis County Recorder and Registrar of Titles handles deeds and certificates of title. About two-thirds of documents recorded there involve abstract property and about one-third involve Torrens property, so ask your title company which kind you have. The county does not offer legal advice or help preparing documents.

Minnesota's state deed tax is 0.33 percent of net consideration under Minnesota Statutes 287.21. You also owe the buyer written disclosure of material facts under Minnesota Statutes 513.55.

Property tax and value appeals

County property tax is due May 15 and October 15. Ask your title company for the current balance before you sign a listing agreement or accept an offer, so nothing about the tax comes as a surprise at closing. If you still owe a balance at the sale, the title company can pay it from your proceeds.

Value appeals follow a set order. Start with the St. Louis County assessor, then go to the city board of appeal and equalization in April or May, then the county board in the last two weeks of June. A Minnesota Tax Court petition must be filed by April 30 of the year the tax is payable.

Selling with a permit, a lease or storm damage

Three situations come up often in Duluth. A vacation rental owner cannot hand a permit to a buyer, so the buyer applies on their own. A landlord should have rental license records ready, because the buyer will ask where the license and inspection stand. A house with roof or foundation damage from winter can still sell, usually to a cash buyer at a price that accounts for repairs.

In each case, tell the buyer up front. Written disclosure of known material facts is required, and surprises discovered after an offer tend to cost more than problems disclosed at the start.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell my Duluth Airbnb with its permit?

No. Existing vacation dwelling units cannot transfer to another owner, and an Interim Use Permit ends when ownership changes or after six years. A buyer must apply under the city's rules, and Planning at 218-730-5580 can explain the current cap and waiting list.

What was the median home sale price in Duluth in 2024?

The median single-family sale price was $295,000, up from $282,350 in 2023. Average time on market was 19 days.

What happens to insurance money on a fire-damaged Duluth house?

Duluth withholds fire escrow funds under Minnesota Statutes 65A.50. Contact Construction Services and Inspections at 218-730-5240 to learn what applies to your property before you sign a sale agreement.

How do I appeal my Duluth property value?

Start by contacting the St. Louis County assessor. If you are not satisfied, appear before the city board of appeal and equalization in April or May, then the county board in the last two weeks of June, and file in Minnesota Tax Court by April 30 of the year the tax is payable.

Does winter make it harder to sell a house in Duluth?

Snow cover usually lasts from late November to early April, so showings happen in tough conditions. Clear walks and roofs, keep the driveway plowed and have heating and insulation records ready, since buyers look closely at winter performance.

Your options for selling in Brooklyn Park

Sellers in this northern suburb tend to weigh three paths against each other. Condition and timing usually settle the choice.

  • Agent listing: the widest audience and normally the top price, paid for with weeks of showings, repair requests and a closing date set by the buyer's bank.
  • Do it yourself: you keep the commission and take on pricing, forms and negotiation.
  • Cash buyer: the fastest close, with the property taken as is. It fits an inherited house, a tenant-occupied one or a place needing repairs, and the offer runs lower in exchange.

Whatever you choose, the new deed gets recorded with Hennepin County, so the closing steps below apply to all three.

Brooklyn Park housing at a glance

Brooklyn Park sits along the Mississippi in northern Hennepin County and is Minnesota's sixth-largest city. The July 2025 estimate is 83,543 residents, 3.4% below the 2020 base. Owners live in 70.3% of homes. Figures for 2020-2024 put the median owner-occupied value at $336,200, median gross rent at $1,325 and median household income at $89,891.

The 2020 census counted 29,656 housing units, 3.1% of them vacant, and the rental vacancy rate was 5.5%. Most land north of 85th Avenue filled in after 2000, so one street map can show 1960s houses next to houses barely two decades old. A buyer sees that spread immediately, and offers react strongly to the age of a roof, furnace or set of windows.

Winters in this part of Minnesota punish roofs, attic insulation and heating equipment. An inspector will study all three, so dig out receipts and service records before the first showing.

Which school district is your address in?

Osseo Area Schools (District 279) covers most of Brooklyn Park. Parts of the city fall in Anoka-Hennepin (District 11) or Robbinsdale (District 281), so the street decides, and you should verify it before writing a listing.

Osseo Senior High and Park Center Senior High are Osseo schools, Champlin Park High is Anoka-Hennepin, and Cooper High is Robbinsdale. Open enrollment lets families choose a school outside their home district. A wrong school name in an ad costs you credibility with buyers, so double-check.

Rental license rules for the next owner

A single-family house in Brooklyn Park that is not lived in by its owner needs a rental license. One exception covers a home rented to an immediate relative who gets a relative homestead exemption. The occupancy cap is four unrelated people.

The city inspects rentals, and the inspection, repairs included, has to be finished before the license renews. Noisy parties, illegal drugs, weapons, assault or other criminal behavior can lead to denial, suspension or revocation. The license holder or designated operator must attend a one-day Crime-free Housing class within a year. The requirement is in Chapter 117.40 of the city code, and the Rental and Business Licensing Division takes questions at 763-493-8182.

An investor buying your house will want the license settled before any tenant moves in. Open maintenance problems lengthen the inspection list.

What closing looks like in Hennepin County

Filing the buyer's deed falls to the Hennepin County Recorder at the Government Center in Minneapolis. Most title companies take care of it on closing day. These are the charges and papers involved.

Any sale above $3,000 also needs an eCRV number. And a parcel with delinquent taxes cannot be transferred, so tax status has to be clean.

Appointments are held on the seventh floor of the A-tower. Other routes are mail and eRecording, which title firms use. Electronic filings post within one to three business days, and mailed originals return in one to two weeks.

Seller disclosure in Minnesota

Before the purchase agreement is signed, you owe the buyer a written statement of the material facts you know that could adversely and significantly affect their use and enjoyment of the property (section 513.55). Write it honestly, from your best knowledge on that day.

For an estate house or a long-vacant one, put down whatever you do know: water in the basement, roof repairs, work done without a city permit. A former rental also sells more smoothly if the items the city checks are already corrected: working smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms within ten feet of bedrooms, handrails on stairs with four or more steps, and working plumbing.

How a cash sale unfolds

The buyer looks at the house as it sits and names a price. If you say yes, a title company opens a file and searches for liens, tax balances or other claims that could block the deed.

With no appraisal or bank approval to wait on, signing is what is left. Your deed and disclosure get executed, any mortgage is paid from the proceeds, Hennepin County receives the deed, and the remainder is yours. Repairs, staging and open houses never happen. Compare the offer with what a listing would leave after fix-up costs and commission.

Before you call a buyer or an agent

An hour of preparation shortens everything that follows. Check which county your tax statement names, confirm the school district for the street, and look up whether the city ever issued a permit for the roof, furnace or finished basement. If the house was a rental, find the last inspection report and the license paperwork.

Next, list what is wrong with the place in plain words. Buyers paying cash price those problems in, so an honest list gets you a steadier offer than one that changes after their walkthrough. Then ask each buyer how long they need to close and whether the offer depends on anything, such as an inspection or financing. A firm date with few conditions is often worth more than a slightly higher number that can fall apart.

What can slow a Brooklyn Park closing?

Unpaid property tax is the usual culprit, because the county will not record a deed until it is cleared. Ask the title company for a payoff figure early. A financed buyer's loan approval is the other common delay. A cash buyer with clean title has no lender step.

Gather your papers ahead of time: the deed or estate documents, tax statements, permit records, and any rental license and inspection reports. A complete folder lets the title company work without stopping to ask for things.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Can a damaged Brooklyn Park house still be sold?

Yes. Cash buyers and investors buy houses with roof, foundation or interior damage, and owners can also list them at a lower price. Material problems you know about still go in the written disclosure.

Who files the deed after a Brooklyn Park closing?

The Hennepin County Recorder, usually through the title company. The package carries the eCRV number, deed tax, the $5 conservation fee and either a well certificate or a well statement.

Do I need a license before renting out my house?

Yes, unless the tenant is an immediate relative who receives a relative homestead. Call the Rental and Business Licensing Division at 763-493-8182 before signing a lease.

Which school district does my Brooklyn Park address belong to?

Probably Osseo Area Schools, District 279. Some addresses are in Anoka-Hennepin (District 11) or Robbinsdale (District 281), so check yours before you name a school in an ad.

What can hold up a Brooklyn Park closing?

Delinquent property tax, which blocks the transfer until paid, and the buyer's loan approval. Paying cash removes the second problem.

Selling a house in Woodbury

Woodbury is one of the pricier east metro suburbs, eight miles east of St. Paul along Interstate 94 in Washington County. Most sales here involve newer houses and active buyers, with a short list of city rules about rentals and permits.

Because the houses are comparatively young, repair problems tend to be smaller than in older cities. The sellers who struggle are usually the ones with a tenant in place, an inherited house far from family, or a deadline that rules out a showing schedule.

Population and housing figures

Woodbury had an estimated 81,558 residents on July 1, 2025, up 8.6% from 75,105 in April 2020. It counted 61,961 people in 2010 and 46,463 in 2000, so the city has grown by about 75% since 2000. Figures for 2020 to 2024:

  • 29,312 households averaging 2.66 people
  • 77.6% of homes owner-occupied
  • Median owner-occupied home value: $450,200
  • Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage: $2,412
  • Median gross rent: $1,908
  • Median household income: $125,310

Families dominate, with 25.8% of residents under 18. High values mean a seller's equity is usually large, so the main question is speed and certainty rather than whether the sale clears the loan.

Neighborhood layout

Woodbury covers 35.722 square miles, of which 34.895 are land. Interstate 94 forms the northern edge, 60th Street South the southern, Century Avenue the west and Manning Avenue the east. Neighbors include Oakdale, Lake Elmo, Cottage Grove, Maplewood, Newport and Afton.

Small lakes dot the city, including Powers, Wilmes, Colby and Carver. Woodbury maintains 63 parks covering about 3,600 acres and around 180 miles of mostly paved trails, which tends to be a selling point for houses near the lakes. Winters and summers are hard on roofs, gutters and furnaces, so expect buyers to ask about them. A quick look at the roof, the gutters and the furnace before you list can head off a price cut during the inspection.

Woodbury rental license rules

Any single family home, townhome or condominium rented in Woodbury needs a city rental license, and the license expires December 31 each year. There is no exemption for owners with only one rental unit. Exceptions exist for family-occupied homes, nursing homes that hold a state license, some contract-for-deed sales while the buyer lives there, a fee waiver for owners on active military duty, and small residential settings with a state license.

Woodbury single-dwelling rental license
License detailWoodbury requirement
2026 license fee$80 per unit

Mid-year additions are pro-rated by quarter. A buyer who plans to keep a tenant should ask the Code Enforcement Division how the license transfers.

Short-term rentals

City code prohibits renting a property for a term shorter than 30 days when the renter's permanent residence is elsewhere. That matters for a buyer who is pricing a house on vacation-rental income, and for a seller whose listing history shows nightly bookings.

Tell any serious buyer about past short-term use up front. The disclosure rules ask sellers to share material facts they know, and a code violation fits that description.

Permits for fixing up a Woodbury house

Woodbury uses a combination permit system. One permit covers building, plumbing, heating and cooling, and electrical fees for additions, basement finishes, decks, porches, remodels, repairs and new construction. Stand-alone flat-fee permits cover single replacements such as a furnace, air conditioner, water heater, water softener or EV charger outlet, and they go to the contractor doing the work or to the homeowner.

  • Applications go through the city's online permitting portal.
  • Residential contractors must hold a valid Minnesota license or a mechanical bond.
  • Morning inspection windows run 9:30 to 11:30 a.m., so call by 9 a.m.
  • Afternoon windows run 1:30 to 3:30 p.m., so call by 1 p.m.

Call the Building Inspections Division at 651-714-3543 if you are unsure whether a project needs a permit. Finish and close any open permits before listing so a buyer's lender doesn't find them.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Woodbury houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Deed tax and recording

The deed is recorded with the Washington County Recorder. Minnesota's deed tax on a sale above $3,000 is .0033 of the net consideration under Minnesota Statutes 287.21, and it is due when the deed is presented for recording.

Your title company normally collects the tax and files the deed. Ask for the figure in the closing statement ahead of time, so you aren't surprised on the day.

A practical order of steps

Decide first whether the house is rented. If it is, confirm the rental license runs through December 31 and note what the buyer needs to do about the transfer. If the house hosted short stays, say so plainly in your disclosure. Close any open permits, then ask the title company for the deed tax figure and the Washington County recording details.

A listing adds showings and a buyer's loan. A cash sale skips them, and Woodbury's high values mean most owners have plenty of equity, so the timing question is mostly about certainty. Inherited houses and houses with a tenant are the usual cases where a buyer who takes the property as is saves the most time.

What a cash sale skips

A traditional sale runs through showings, an offer, the buyer's loan approval and a lender's appraisal before the closing date is even set. A cash sale drops the loan and appraisal. The buyer's title company still checks the owner of record, any liens and the taxes, and the deed still gets recorded in Washington County, so the paperwork above doesn't go away. What goes away is the waiting on a lender.

For a seller with a tenant, an inherited house or a firm deadline, that can be the difference between a closing you can plan around and one that slips. For a seller with a clean, updated house and time, a listing may bring a higher price. Ask for both numbers before you choose, and compare what you would net after fees, repairs and the time the house sits.

Lakeville market overview

Lakeville is the largest city in Dakota County, with 79,270 residents, about 20 miles south of both downtown Minneapolis and downtown St. Paul along Interstate 35. It grew 14.1 percent between April 2020 and mid-2025, and it covers about 36 square miles. New construction keeps arriving alongside resales, so a seller competes with fresh builds as well as other used houses.

The median owner-occupied home is valued at $452,500, and owners live in 87.8 percent of housing units. The city has 25,685 households averaging 2.89 people. Median household income is $139,041, owners with a mortgage pay a median $2,437 a month, and the commute averages 23.6 minutes. Median gross rent is $1,806, which is worth weighing if your house could be rented out instead of sold.

Interstate 35 is the main artery, and Cedar Avenue (Minnesota Highway 77) runs along the east side.

Rental and short-term rental rules

These rules matter if the house is rented now or you are thinking of renting it first. Since September 2023 Lakeville has required registration of long-term rentals, meaning stays of 32 days or longer. Registration is free and one-time unless contact information or ownership changes, and the city does not require inspections. An owner with several rentals files a form for each property.

Short-term rentals are allowed only with a Short-Term Rental Administrative Permit under Title 9, Chapter 10 of city code.

  • Listings must show the city permit number, maximum occupancy and maximum number of vehicles.
  • Overnight guests are capped at two adults per bedroom plus their dependent children.
  • Guest vehicles park in the garage or on the driveway, and noise must be reduced between 10:00 PM and 7:00 AM.
  • Owners pay local lodging tax under Title 3, Chapter 17 of city code.

A buyer who wants to run a rental after closing will ask whether the property is registered, so file the registration if you still hold the house as a rental.

Choosing how to sell

  • Full-service listing: makes sense when the house is current on maintenance and you can accept showings, appraisal timing and the buyer's financing conditions.
  • Direct cash sale: fits a house with deferred repairs, a probate or inherited property, or a rental where the lease complicates showings.
  • Selling it yourself: removes the agent fee but puts disclosures and negotiation on you.

Winters here are cold, so roof, furnace and insulation condition tend to draw buyer questions. Gather service records for those systems before you open the house to buyers. If the sale involves an inherited house, ask a title company whether the estate needs court paperwork before the deed can be signed.

Which school district is my house in?

Most Lakeville households are in Lakeville Area School District 194, which runs Lakeville North and Lakeville South high schools. Parts of northern and eastern Lakeville fall under District 196 (Rosemount-Apple Valley-Eagan) or Farmington District 192.

Because the boundaries date from the farming era, two neighbors can be in different districts. Minnesota's open enrollment law also lets families choose a school outside their home district. Name the exact district for the address in your listing so buyers do not have to guess.

Stopping Lakeville utilities

Lakeville bills residential water quarterly and calculates sewer charges from winter-quarter water use. The city's Form Center has an online stop-service form for sellers and a start-service form for buyers. You can pay bills through InvoiceCloud, by mail, or at City Hall at 20195 Holyoke Avenue. Call the Utility Division at 952-985-2700 with questions about the meter, and ask for a final read that matches your closing date.

Dakota County Property Taxation and Records records Lakeville deeds at its Hastings office. State deed tax is 0.0033 of the net price. A tenant in place changes the timeline. Showings need notice, and a lease may run past the day a retail buyer wants to move in. Read the lease for its end date and any renewal option, then decide whether to wait it out, offer the tenant a move-out agreement, or sell to a buyer who will keep the renter. Hand over the lease, the rent history and the city registration so the buyer sees a clean file. Security deposits transfer or are returned at closing, so settle that with the title company in writing.

Selling a newer house against new construction

Because builders keep adding homes, buyers can compare your house with a brand-new one down the road. Lean on what a resale offers: a finished yard, mature landscaping and a known street. Note any updates to the kitchen, roof or furnace with dates. If the house needs work that would cost more than a retail buyer will credit, an as-is cash offer lets you skip the comparison and the repair bill.

Prepare the property before buyers arrive

Walk the lot as a buyer would. Fix loose railings, clear the gutters, test smoke detectors and make sure the furnace and water heater run. List any known leaks or past water in the basement, because the disclosure covers what you know. Keep the list short, specific and dated, and attach receipts where you have them. It is better for a buyer to read about an old repair from you than to find it during an inspection.

Keep your latest tax statement, the parcel number, any rental registration and the keys together. Schedule the water meter read, ask the county for a payoff if taxes are owed, and confirm with the title company who files the deed. If tenants live in the house, give the buyer the lease and the registration details. A cash buyer can often work around a lease, which a retail buyer usually cannot. At closing you sign the deed, hand over keys and garage openers, and receive your proceeds after the title company pays off any mortgage and taxes owed.

State deed tax is 0.0033 of the net price above $3,000. Your title company will show the exact figure on the closing statement.

Who do I contact to stop Lakeville utilities when I sell?

Use the Finance forms on the city's Form Center to stop service, or contact the Utility Division at 952-985-2700. Bills are quarterly, so ask for a final read that matches your closing date.

Plymouth skews toward owners and expensive homes, about 10 miles west of downtown Minneapolis. The 2025 estimate is 2.6% below the April 2020 base, so demand is steady and not climbing fast, and roughly 89% of residents were at the same address the year before.

Getting the house ready for an inspector

Winters are cold, with average lows near 3 degrees Fahrenheit. Inspectors go straight to the roof, gutters, attic insulation and furnace, so look at those yourself before the first showing. A direct buyer checks the same items and prices them in, so a short list of known problems helps whichever route you take.

If your Plymouth house is a rental

Every Plymouth rental needs a rental dwelling license, from a single-family home to a large complex. One- and two-family homes and condominium units get a three-year license, and other dwelling types renew each year.

City inspectors visit apartment buildings annually and other rental housing every three years. An owner or manager with more than one Plymouth rental has to complete Crime Free Multi-Housing training before renewal. Licenses cannot be transferred or refunded, which means a buyer keeping your tenant must apply in the buyer's own name. Phone the city's Community and Economic Development department at 763-509-5430 for the current fee schedule and for the timing of your next inspection.

The city also has a lodging tax ordinance that applies to short-term rentals. Did you rent the house by the night? Ask the city how that tax applies before closing.

Before the purchase agreement is signed, Minnesota Statutes section 513.55 has you put in writing the facts you know that could significantly hurt an ordinary buyer's enjoyment of the home. Write it honestly, from your own knowledge.

At closing, Hennepin County's recording office expects the deed, an electronic certificate of real estate value when the price tops $3,000, a "send tax statements to" address and the well statement.

Property taxes at closing

Plymouth's property tax bill from Hennepin County comes due in spring and fall, on the 15th of May and of October. When the 15th lands on a weekend or holiday, payment is due the following business day. Before you list, confirm the most recent payment posted.

Late payments draw a state penalty that grows each month on the unpaid part. If a lender escrows your taxes, ask the servicer for payoff and escrow refund figures well ahead of closing. The title company then divides the current year's bill by ownership dates. The county's tax payment page explains payment methods, and the property tax line at 612-348-3011 can confirm a parcel's status. If the bill is paid through escrow, you may be owed a refund from the servicer after closing, so keep the servicer's address current. If you pay the bill yourself, keep the receipt for each half, since the title company will ask which payments are already made and a quick answer keeps the closing date on track.

From accepted offer to closing day

After you accept a direct offer, the title company runs the search and prepares the deed. Your part is the well statement, an address for future tax statements and a payoff figure from your lender. A rented house also needs the lease details and the license expiration date handed over. At closing the deed is recorded, the year's tax is divided by ownership dates, and you are paid what is left once your mortgage and any unpaid tax are settled. Ask the title company for a copy of the final statement and keep it with your tax records for next year's filing, along with the recorded deed once it comes back.

Do I have to fix anything before selling my Plymouth house?

No, a house can sell in its present condition. You must still give the buyer a written list of material problems you know about. Conventional buyers negotiate over inspection results, while a direct buyer folds repair costs into the price and closes with no fixes from you.

Will my Plymouth rental license pass to the buyer?

No. It cannot be transferred, and the new owner applies for a fresh one. Tell the buyer when yours expires and when the next city inspection falls due.

Which office records a Plymouth deed?

Hennepin County's Recorder and Registrar of Titles, not city hall. Book a time at the Government Center in Minneapolis, mail the deed, have your title company eRecord it, or file online for a $3 service fee.

What if my Plymouth home has back property tax?

The tax and penalties have to be paid before the deed will be recorded, and the title company normally handles that at the closing. Hennepin County's property tax line, 612-348-3011, can give an exact figure.

How do I find out which school district my Plymouth address belongs to?

Ask the district itself. Wayzata, Robbinsdale, Osseo and Hopkins each cover part of Plymouth, with Wayzata taking most of the city. Have the answer ready before your first showing, because buyers with children will ask.

Population stands at 76,603, a 9.1 percent gain since April 2020 and the biggest total in Anoka County. Most of it lies in Anoka County and a piece reaches into Ramsey County. Commuters and families make up most of the buyer pool. For 2020 to 2024, 85.3 percent of homes are owner-occupied and the typical home is valued at $352,400. Monthly cost for owners with a mortgage is $2,008, median gross rent is $1,705, and median household income is $106,801. The same-house rate is 90.4 percent, so owners here tend to stay put. Test any offer against the recent sale of a comparable house in your own subdivision.

Documents to gather in Blaine

About three weeks ahead of listing, collect the documents the other side will want. Start with the tax statement, which shows your parcel number and the county that taxes it. Find the sump pump records, repair receipts and any radon test results you hold. If tenants live in the house, locate the rental license, the last inspection result and the leases.

Then draft the written disclosure. Hand it over before the purchase agreement is signed. Writing it early means you can reply the day an offer lands. If the house needs repairs you do not want to make, say so plainly in the disclosure and price accordingly. A cash buyer who takes the house as it stands will still read that document, so it is the one piece of paperwork worth getting right. Sellers who skip the early gathering usually end up scrambling for permits, lease copies or repair receipts in the middle of a closing week, and that scramble is what stretches a quick sale into a slow one. Spring Lake Park Schools covers nearly everything south of 99th Avenue NE, and Centennial Schools covers the area east of Lexington Avenue and south and east of Interstate 35W.

Lines follow streets, not neighborhoods, so neighbors a block apart may fall in separate districts. Check your address with the district before you quote one to a buyer.

Blaine licenses rental property every year, and a buyer who inherits your tenants takes on that duty. The license expires on December 31, and owners with three consecutive years without violations qualify for a reduced fee.

A Certificate of Real Estate Value is due at the auditor's office when a property sells, as Minnesota Statute 272.115 requires. A qualifying disabled veteran can receive a market value exclusion of up to $300,000 on homestead property, so buyers who qualify may ask about it. Disclosures a Blaine seller owes

Under Minnesota Statute 513.55, you must write down any material facts you know that could adversely and significantly affect a buyer's use and enjoyment, and you must do it before signing the purchase agreement. Section 144.496 adds a radon disclosure: whether tests were done, the latest reports, any mitigation system, a radon warning statement and the Minnesota Department of Health booklet.

Blaine sits on glacial sand, ponds and wetlands, so basement moisture is a fair thing to document. Gather any sump pump records, past repairs and test results before the first showing so the written disclosure is accurate and complete.

After you accept a Blaine offer

When the offer is signed, the title company reviews the land record, requests tax figures and drafts a deed that covers each checklist item. You can list with an agent, sell the house yourself, or take a cash offer from a buyer who accepts the property as is. All three need the same groundwork: Minnesota's written seller disclosure, clear title, any open city permits closed, and a closing date that fits your move.

The city counts 73,893 residents, up 5.2 percent from 2020, and 82.3 percent of homes have their owners living in them. A house needing work can still sell, but fewer buyers can take on repairs than can buy a move-in-ready home.

  • Agent: a good match for a tidy house if weeks of showings do not bother you.
  • Owner sale: you handle marketing, disclosure and the purchase agreement.
  • Cash: quicker closing, with repairs left to the buyer and priced in.

Housing and income in Maple Grove

Incomes in this Hennepin County suburb run high: the median household makes $132,731, and the usual owner-occupied house is worth $418,300. Median gross rent is $1,868 and owners with a mortgage pay a median $2,303 a month. The city has 27,811 households of about 2.55 people each, and the average commute is 24.0 minutes.

Buyers reach the city by Interstate 94 and U.S. Highway 169, with Highway 610 across the north. Most addresses are in Osseo Area School District 279, and Wayzata Public Schools serves a portion, so look up the district for your street before you advertise. Lakeside or in a newer subdivision, the house will be priced against nearby sales, so keep your own numbers handy.

Permits and licenses that matter at a sale

Permits are filed online through the city's ePermits system. One is needed before a building is built, enlarged, altered, repaired, moved or demolished. Residential plan review can take one or two weeks, and a permit expires after 180 days if no work starts or no inspection is called in.

A buyer's title and inspection work can turn up open or expired permits. If you are unsure what is on file for your address, call Building Inspections.

It lasts one year, comes only after an inspection and a training presentation, and requires the owner's name on the application to match state property records. Hennepin County taxes and deed tax

Hennepin County sends two bills a year to Maple Grove owners, due May 15 and October 15. A due date on a non-business day moves to the next business day. Valuation notices arrive in March using the assessor's January 2 value, and tax statements come the following March. For questions, Hennepin's tax line is 612-348-3011.

Deed tax is a state charge due when the deed goes in for recording. Minnesota Statutes 287.21 sets it at 0.33 percent of net consideration over $3,000, with a flat $1.65 for transfers at or below that amount. The closing agent usually collects it, and the purchase agreement names who pays.

Your bill reflects levies from the county, city, school district and other taxing districts. Two school districts share the city, so find out which one taxes your parcel.

Roofs, storms and older homes

Snowy winters lead buyers of older homes to ask about roof age, gutters and drainage, and these are easier to photograph once the ground is clear. Save the paperwork for any roof job. A dated receipt settles the question quickly.

Hennepin County maintains most of the larger roads, including County Road 10 (Bass Lake Road), County Road 30, Hemlock Lane and Weaver Lake Road. A house on one of those corridors deals with county road projects as well as city ones, so mention any planned work you know about.

Is a cash offer worth considering?

Cash makes sense if you need a firm closing date, own a dated house, or inherited a place you would rather not fix up. At $418,300 typical value, repair bills here can run large, and a buyer who absorbs them may save you time even at a lower number.

Get the figure in writing and line it up against a realistic listing: what you would net after repairs, staging and the months of carrying the house. Settle who pays title charges, who signs a well disclosure if the lot has a well, and how funds reach you at closing.

Disclosure items to think through

The written disclosure must be in the buyer's hands before the purchase agreement is signed. Run through basement water, roof leaks, sewer backups, unpermitted work and any city notice. If the lot has a well, the disclosure includes a statement and map. Being specific protects you, since a seller who knew of a defect and stayed silent can face a claim later. A cash buyer will still ask the same questions, so the list is useful whichever way you sell.

Timing a Maple Grove sale around your move

Work backward from the day you need to be out. A listing needs time to prepare, show and wait on a buyer's lender, and a repair request after the inspection can restart the clock. A cash sale lets you pick a date and skip that sequence, which helps when you are buying a new home, relocating for a job or settling an estate. Whichever way you go, confirm the last day you can stay and what condition the buyer expects the house to be left in. Say whether appliances, window coverings and the shed stay. Put those details in the purchase agreement so nothing is argued at the final walk-through, and keep copies of every signed page.

What to have ready

Pull together your tax statement, permit records, survey and big-repair receipts before the first showing. Find out whether the lot has a well or a private sewer system, because both bring extra disclosure steps. If you rent the house, have the lease and license papers on hand. A buyer, whether retail or cash, will ask for these before making a firm offer, and a ready folder shortens the time to closing.

Which city office handles permit questions for a Maple Grove property?

Building Inspections at 763-494-6060 can look up your address. Permits expire 180 days after issuance if no work starts or no inspection is called in, and an open permit is worth closing before you list.

What is the Minnesota deed tax on a Maple Grove sale?

The rate is 0.33 percent of net consideration over $3,000, payable at recording. Your purchase agreement sets which party covers it.

What are the Hennepin County payment dates for a Maple Grove house?

May 15 for the first half and October 15 for the second half. A non-business 15th pushes the deadline to the following business day.

Can I sell a Maple Grove house that is currently a short-term rental?

Yes. Maple Grove requires a license for any rental under 30 days, valid for one year and issued after an inspection, so a buyer who wants to keep renting short term should confirm the license steps with Community and Economic Development at 763-494-6040.

Which school district serves my Maple Grove house?

Most of the city is in Osseo Area School District 279, and part is in Wayzata Public Schools. Check your address with the district before you list.

Selling a house quickly in St. Cloud

You can sell through an agent, find your own buyer, or take a cash offer from someone who buys as-is. Cash tends to fit houses with repairs, tenants or a title problem, while a listing fits a tidy house when you have time to spare.

St. Cloud is a rental-heavy market. Only 48.6 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, and a typical owner's home is valued at $225,000. Many sellers own an investment house or inherited one, so the rental and vacancy rules below come up here more than in a typical suburb.

  • List when the house shows well and you can wait for a buyer's mortgage to clear.
  • Sell yourself when you have a buyer lined up and are comfortable with the paperwork.
  • Choose cash when a rental license, a vacant house, repairs or an estate make a conventional sale slow.

Which county your St. Cloud parcel is in

St. Cloud is the seat of Stearns County, and the city also reaches into Benton and Sherburne counties. It sits on both banks of the Mississippi River, about 65 miles northwest of the Twin Cities, and Interstate 94, U.S. Highways 10 and 52, and State Highways 15 and 23 serve it.

  • Counties: because parcels sit in up to three counties, find your parcel's county before asking about taxes or records.
  • Schools: most of the city is in the St. Cloud Area School District, and part of the Benton County portion is in Sauk Rapids-Rice Public Schools.
  • Nearby campuses: St. Cloud State University and St. Cloud Technical and Community College are in the city, which keeps student rentals in steady demand.

Housing and income figures

The population estimate for July 1, 2025 is 72,647, up 4.4 percent from 69,618 in April 2020. There are 27,807 households, and median gross rent is $1,003 a month. About 77.1 percent of residents were in the same house a year earlier, so roughly one in four people moved within or into the city in a single year.

Rental licenses and training

Any owner who lets a property be occupied in exchange for rent or other goods or services needs a St. Cloud rental license. Getting the license also requires rental training, so a seller who bought a house to rent should confirm it is current before a buyer asks.

The training is free and virtual, taught by the Police, Fire and Health departments, and it covers St. Cloud ordinances and policies. After signing up, an owner has three months to finish it. The property owner, manager or another person in charge of the unit can attend. Questions go to the Police Department's information desk at 320-345-4444.

  • Pre-rental license application: on the Housing and Code Enforcement page for owners starting a rental.

Stearns County taxes and records

Property tax and recording questions go to the county where the parcel sits, usually Stearns County. Its Auditor-Treasurer pages cover tax due dates, penalties, payment options, relief options and a senior citizen property tax deferral, and its assessor publishes an annual assessment update.

For a house in the Benton or Sherburne portion, call that county's treasurer instead. Whichever county applies, ask for the payoff on both halves of the current year and any special assessments, and ask the county recorder what the deed and any certificate of real estate value must include.

  • Taxes: ask the Auditor-Treasurer for current and delinquent balances in writing before closing.
  • Assessment: ask the assessor whether a recent remodel, permit or new addition changed the value.
  • Utility bills: the city's Health and Inspections pages link to utility billing, and an unpaid balance is worth settling before the sale.

Many St. Cloud sales involve more than one of these offices, so list them before you start. A parcel in the Benton or Sherburne portion is where mistakes happen, because the wrong county's office will answer from the wrong records.

Selling an older house in St. Cloud

Buyers often ask how a house has been used, whether as an owner's home, a rental with a city license or a vacant property, so the paper trail matters. Keep the license, inspection papers and any permits for the house in one place.

The city handles complaint response and routine rental inspections through its Housing and Code Enforcement division, and it publishes information sheets on accessory structures, fences, off-street parking and recreational vehicles. Check those items on your own lot. A shed, fence or parked trailer that breaks the rules is easy to fix before an inspection, and a clean lot helps a buyer picture the house in good order.

The city also publishes a flyer on bed bugs for owners. If a rental has had a past infestation, have the treatment records ready to show a buyer.

Steps for a quick St. Cloud sale

Work through the offices in a sensible order. First confirm the county for your parcel. Second, get the tax balance on both halves and any special assessments. Third, if the house is a rental, pull the license and the proof that rental training was finished. Fourth, if it is vacant, look at the vacant property registration. Fifth, ask a title company or the county recorder what the deed needs, and settle any utility balance.

A listing adds showings, a buyer's loan and an appraisal. A cash sale skips them, so the timeline mostly follows the title work and the county paperwork. A buyer paying cash can take the house with tenants in place or after they move out, which is why many owners of St. Cloud rentals and inherited houses pick that route. If the buyer will keep the tenants, hand over the lease terms and the license so the sale is not held up by questions. If the house will be empty at closing, plan a move-out date and confirm the utilities are paid through that date.
