Recording the deed in Washington County

Your buyer's deed is filed with the Washington County Recorder, whose office is in the Government Center in Stillwater. Expect a $46 recording charge and state deed tax of $3.30 for each thousand dollars of the price. A $5 conservation fee is added, and a $54 well certificate is needed when the deed does not carry a well statement. When the price is under $3,000 the tax is a flat $1.65. Certain deeds also require an electronic Certificate of Real Estate Value.

The county reminds parties that most parcels here are abstract property, which makes a careful title search worth doing before closing. Research staff in the Government Center keep weekday hours from 8 a.m. to 4:15 p.m. Separately, Minnesota Statutes 103I.235 requires you to give the buyer a written note about any wells you know of before you sign.

A short checklist for Cottage Grove sellers

Four items come up in nearly every sale here. Pull the permit record for roofing, windows and any finished space. Order a PFAS test if you rely on a private well. Ask the city for the utility estimate through your closing agent. Confirm the tax balance and which installment has been paid.

Hand that folder to each buyer you talk to. A buyer who sees clean records can price quickly, and one who sees gaps will discount the offer or ask for time. If you do not want to spend weeks fixing gaps, a cash buyer will take the house as it is, with the discount built into the number.

Property taxes when you sell

Tax on most real property comes due in two equal halves, May 15 and October 15. Values are set as of January 2. By March 31 the county mails statements along with a valuation notice for the following year, and a Proposed Property Tax Notice goes out in mid-November.

A homestead that misses the first-half date is charged a 2 percent penalty starting May 16. Anything still unpaid on January 2 turns delinquent and accrues 8 percent annual interest. Payment options are eCheck at $0.75, card at 2.35 percent, mail, bank bill pay or the Government Center drop box. To discuss your value, call an assessor at 651-430-6175.

When taxes are owed at the sale, the title company can pay them from your proceeds at closing, so ask for the balance early.

Can I get my private well tested for PFAS in Cottage Grove?

Yes. Cottage Grove is among the east metro communities where the state samples private wells, and sampling of eligible wells is free to homeowners. Use the online request form on the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency's well sampling page.

Who pays the city utility bill at a Cottage Grove closing?

You do, from your proceeds. The closing company asks the city for an estimate on its Utility Billing Request for Real Estate Closing form and settles current and outstanding amounts at the table.

What are the deed recording costs in Washington County?

A $46 recording charge, deed tax of $3.30 per thousand dollars of price, and a $5 conservation fee. Add $54 for a well certificate if the deed has no well statement.

When are Washington County property taxes due?

In two halves, May 15 and October 15. A homestead that pays the first half late is charged 2 percent starting May 16.

Do I need a permit to replace the roof or windows before selling in Cottage Grove?

Yes. Roofing, siding, window replacement and door replacement are all on the city's residential permit list, and applications go through the online permitting site. Call 651-458-2800 or email building@cottagegrovemn.gov for help with an account.

Selling in Maplewood: the order of steps

Maplewood adds a local step before anything else: a Truth-in-Sale of Housing evaluation has to be done before the house is shown. After that you choose an agent, a sale on your own or a cash buyer. The evaluation sits on top of Minnesota's disclosure rules, and it sets how fast you can go to market.

The city is in Ramsey County, on the northern and eastern edge of Saint Paul, about ten minutes' drive from downtown. The latest estimate of 40,717 residents is 3.2 percent below the 2020 count. Owners hold 71.8 percent of homes. The typical owner-occupied house is valued at $323,200, rent is $1,406 and household income is $91,394, across 15,210 households.

  • Agent listing: evaluation first, then showings with the report on display.
  • Owner sale: same city report, plus your own disclosures and contract.
  • Cash sale: the buyer purchases in present condition, and the report is still part of the file.

What the Truth-in-Sale report covers

Single-family houses, duplexes, townhouses, condominiums and other attached one-family units need a full report before they can be shown. A duplex needs a report for each unit. Manufactured homes are not covered. The city's Truth-in-Sale page has the program details.

You call a evaluator the city approves yourself, since each evaluator sets fees and availability. The evaluator files a copy with the city and gives you one, which you keep on display for buyers. A copy must go to the buyer before a contract is signed, and the report is valid for one owner or one year.

The owner also signs a statement covering:

  • Flooding, sewer backup or chronic water seepage the owner knows about, and its cause and extent.
  • Pending housing orders from the city, and whether the home has a homestead classification.
  • Known wells, with a map, and whether each is in use or sealed.
  • Deed restrictions, shoreland, pipeline or floodplain rules, and an adjacent high-voltage transmission line.

The report is for disclosure, and the sale does not depend on the deficiencies it lists. City inspectors may still use it to require correction of code violations.

Well disclosure under state law

Before you sign an agreement to sell, Minnesota Statutes 103I.235 requires a written statement that you know of no wells, or a statement and map showing each well and whether it is in use, not in use or sealed. At closing, a well disclosure certificate goes to the recorder unless the deed carries the standard no-wells statement.

The county recorder collects $54 for a completed certificate. A seller who knew of an undisclosed well can owe the sealing costs and attorney fees if the buyer sues within six years of closing. Individual condominium units are exempt. If you are unsure whether an old well exists on your lot, check your survey and deed records before you sign.

Ramsey County taxes

Ramsey County splits the bill into a May 15 payment and an October 15 payment, and a weekend due date rolls forward to the next business day. Real property tax of $100 or less must be paid in full by May 15. A homestead penalty starts at 2 percent on the day after the first half is due and climbs to 4 percent on June 1.

The county allows a one-time penalty waiver once every ten years for each parcel, applying to either the first or the second half. Hardship abatement requests go to the Auditor/Treasurer's office at 651-266-2222. Valuation questions go to the county assessor at 651-266-2131.

The assessor's estimated market value is set as of January 2 for taxes payable the following year. If you sell in the second half of the year, ask the closing agent how the October installment will be divided, since the purchase agreement controls it.

Owning a rental in Maplewood

Since 2019 Maplewood has required a rental license before tenants move in, with a background check on each owner and an on-site inspection. Properties are placed on a one-, two- or three-year inspection cycle.

How to line up the evaluation

Book the evaluator early. Compare quotes and ask how soon a report can be filed, since showings cannot begin until it exists. Walk the house first and fix the cheap items, so the report is shorter. If the report lists problems, you can repair them, leave them for the buyer to handle or price them into an as-is sale. A cash buyer will read the same report and adjust the offer.

Keep the filed copy where visitors can see it, and give the buyer their copy before any contract is signed. Missing that step can delay the whole sale.

Questions buyers ask about older Maplewood houses

Neighborhoods built from the 1950s onward replaced farmsteads, so many houses carry decades of updates and repairs. Buyers ask about the roof, the furnace, the water heater, the sewer line and any basement moisture. Write the answers down with dates before the evaluator arrives, because the report and your disclosure should tell the same story. If a seller statement and an evaluator's findings disagree, a buyer notices, and the sale slows.

Since owners here stay put for years, many sellers have never gone through a sale under the current rules. Walk through each step once, from the evaluation to the deed, so no document is a surprise on closing day. Ask your title company early for a list of what it will need from you, including the tax statement, the evaluation report and the well statement, and return each item promptly.

What a cash sale means in Maplewood

A cash buyer purchases the house in its present condition, but the city report still has to exist, so book the evaluator first. The advantage is speed and certainty: you skip the lender's appraisal, repair negotiations and most showings. Ask for the offer in writing with a firm closing date, then compare it with what a listing would net after repairs and carrying costs. On closing day the title company records the deed and pays any mortgage and taxes owed from your proceeds.

Does Maplewood require an inspection before I can list my house?

Yes. An evaluator the city approves must complete a Truth-in-Sale of Housing report before the property is shown. It covers houses, duplexes, townhouses and condominiums, and you call the evaluator directly to book it.

How long does a Maplewood TISH report last?

One owner or one year. The city's director can also require a new inspection if there is substandard maintenance or later damage to the building.

Do I have to repair everything on the Maplewood report before selling?

No. The sale does not depend on the deficiencies listed, though inspectors may use the report to require correction of code violations later.

What are the Ramsey County payment dates for a Maplewood home?

May 15 and October 15. A homestead pays a 2 percent penalty if the first half arrives after May 15, and Ramsey offers a one-time waiver per parcel every ten years.

What does a Maplewood rental license cost?

The annual fee is $150 plus $50 per unit, and each owner passes a background check and an inspection before the license is issued.

Inver Grove Heights housing basics

Inver Grove Heights is a Dakota County city of 36,873 people covering about 27.9 square miles. It lies roughly nine miles southeast of Saint Paul, with Newport and Saint Paul Park across the Mississippi River. Interstate 494, U.S. 52 and Minnesota Highways 55 and 3 are the main roads.

Of all housing units, 76.9 percent are lived in by their owners, and the middle value is $363,400. The city has 15,158 households of 2.35 people each, rent is $1,465 at the median, household income is $101,316 and the commute averages 22.3 minutes.

Ways to sell an Inver Grove Heights house

Inver Grove Heights changed its short-term rental rules effective April 1, 2025. If the owner does not live there, the minimum rental stay is 30 days, Airbnb and Vrbo listings included. Shorter stays are allowed only when the home is owner-occupied.

Long-term rentals need a city rental license. The city has been revising the license term, renewal deadline and manager rules, so the clerk is the person to ask about current terms when you sell a rented house. A buyer who will keep renting wants the license history, so collect it first.

Which school district is my house in?

Selling an inherited house

Heirs often sell here. Before anyone signs a deed, ask a title company which court papers prove who may sell. Collect the death certificate, the will if one exists, and the newest tax statement. Once you accept an offer, the title company runs a search, drafts the deed and sets the closing. At closing you sign, hand over keys and receive your proceeds once any mortgage and taxes are paid.

Preparing the house for showings or a buyer visit

Even in an as-is sale, a little attention pays off. Clear the walkways, cut the grass, put away stored vehicles and remove brush piles so the lot does not draw a code notice while buyers are looking. Turn on the lights, open the blinds and make sure the buyer can reach the furnace, water heater and electrical panel. Keep receipts for any recent roof, furnace or plumbing work in one folder to hand over.

What a cash sale skips

With cash there is no cleaning, no repair list and no staging, and no lender appraisal, which is the usual cause of closing delays. Only if sewage on the property does not go to a permitted facility. Under Minnesota Statutes 115.55, you must then describe the system and map it before the purchase agreement is signed.

The Richfield Point of Sale inspection

Richfield requires a city housing inspection before title passes on any single-family home, two-family home or condominium. The council adopted the Point of Sale program in 1989 for transfers after October 1, 1990, and the city issues a Certificate of Housing Maintenance that has to be in hand at closing.

That rule shapes every sale in the city, whether you list the house, sell it yourself or sell directly to an investor. The inspection has to happen before closing, and any repairs it turns up must be finished and re-inspected before closing and within one year of the first visit. The city recommends scheduling the inspection before the house is listed or advertised, and the owner, not the agent, is responsible for arranging it. A city housing inspector does the work. You apply online, pay the fee, and only then call the inspections line at 612-861-9882 to book a time.

Richfield Point of Sale inspection fees (include one initial inspection and one re-inspection)
Property typeFee
Single-family home$190
Two-family home$270
Condominium$140

No inspection is needed when a name is only being removed from title after a divorce or a death and no sale is happening.

What inspectors look for and who pays for repairs

The inspector looks at the roof, foundation, doors and windows, exterior covering, electrical, plumbing, chimney and heating and cooling, then gives you a written list. The program does not force older houses up to today's code. It requires fixes for violations of the code in force when the house was built and for anything unsafe.

  • Missing or dead smoke detectors, loose or absent handrails, and first-floor windows without locks.
  • Bare wood or peeling paint, damaged window screens, cracked glass and clogged or missing gutters.
  • Furnaces more than 15 years old or installed without a permit, which need certification by a heating contractor.
  • Electrical or plumbing changes with no permit on file, which need a certification from an electrician or plumber.
  • Ungrounded three-prong outlets, extension cords used as permanent wiring and vinyl or foil dryer vents.

An owner who lives in the home can often do the repairs personally, as long as the work meets code. If you would rather not do them, the buyer can take over the work order, submit a schedule, agree on when hazards will be removed and sign a Housing Cash Escrow Agreement with the city. The certificate is not a warranty, and the city says it is no substitute for a private inspection.

Housing stock and remodeling loans

Richfield is an inner-ring suburb that touches Minneapolis on the north, the airport and Fort Snelling on the east, Bloomington on the south and Edina on the west. Most of its roughly 10,000 single-family houses went up in the 1950s, and its 5,000 or so apartments date from the 1960s and early 1970s.

The common corrections listed above are heavy on wiring, furnaces and windows. Several remodeling programs can help owners get ahead of that. A Fix Up loan through the Center for Energy and the Environment runs from $2,000 to $35,000. The Transformation Home Loan covers 15% of a project that costs $50,000 or more, up to $25,000, with no payments and no interest.

Check for these loans before you sell. The Transformation Home Loan comes due on sale of the home or is forgiven after 30 years, and Hennepin County's Deferred Loan, up to $30,000 for qualifying households, is also due on sale or forgiven after 15 years. Look through your records for either one so the payoff shows on the title company's closing statement.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Richfield house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Richfield housing snapshot

Richfield leans toward renters. Only 61.6% of homes are lived in by their owners, and the typical household is small at 2.19 people. Estimated population for July 2025 is 36,593, which is 1.1% fewer than the 2020 base.

Owners value the middle home at $344,000, renters pay a median of $1,393 and the median household earns $85,132. Richfield Public Schools (ISD 280) serve the city and part of Edina, so name the district when you advertise.

Rental license and inspection

Every residential rental in Richfield needs a city license and an inspection each year under City Code Section 407. License renewals are due by December 31, so a rental sold in the fall or winter needs a renewal plan.

  • Apply to the city for the license.
  • Schedule an inspection of the interior, exterior and common areas.
  • Correct any violations within the timeframe the report gives.
  • Renew each year.

The rental license fee covers two inspections. Further visits cost more, starting at $50 for the third inspection of a one- or two-unit building and climbing to a cap of $1,500, and $100 to $3,000 for buildings with three or more units.

Section 409 gives tenants in affordable units a three-month protection period when a building changes hands, and the new owner's notice is due a month after the transfer. Owners of one- to three-unit buildings are also responsible for unpaid organized trash collection charges once balances reach $100, which the city can assess to property taxes. Settle that account before the closing date.

Hennepin County deed and property tax

Hennepin County records the deed and bills the property tax. Property tax arrives in two installments, with deadlines on May 15 and October 15. When the 15th is a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves forward.

When the sale closes, your title company submits the deed along with the electronic certificate of real estate value, a statement naming where tax statements go and the well statement or certificate. Parcels with delinquent taxes cannot be transferred. The recording fee is $46 per document and the well certificate is $54. Under Minnesota Statutes section 513.55, you also give the buyer a written disclosure before the purchase agreement is signed. Title companies and lenders can use the county's eRecord system, which records documents within one to three days. You can read the full fee list on the county's recording page.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Richfield houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

A practical order of steps

Book the Point of Sale inspection first, since it sets the pace for everything else. Apply online, pay the fee, and call to schedule. When the report arrives, decide which repairs you will do and which the buyer will take over under the escrow agreement. Clear any trash collection balance and check for remodeling loans. Then confirm taxes are current so the deed can be recorded, and give the buyer the written disclosure before the agreement is signed.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell my Richfield house to an investor and skip the city inspection?

No. The Point of Sale requirement applies to the transfer of title, so it covers every sale of a single-family home, two-family home or condominium, whoever the buyer is. The buyer can take over repairs under a Housing Cash Escrow Agreement.

How long is a Richfield Point of Sale inspection good for?

Repairs must be completed and re-inspected before closing and within one year of the first inspection. Plan the inspection so your closing date falls inside that year.

What does the Richfield Point of Sale fee include?

It covers one initial inspection and one re-inspection. The fee is $190 for a single-family home, $270 for a two-family home and $140 for a condominium.

Does Richfield's rental license transfer with the house?

Roseville at a glance

Roseville is an inner-ring suburb in Ramsey County that borders both Saint Paul and Minneapolis. About 35,663 people live here as of July 1, 2025, a little under the 36,268 counted in 2020. The population skews older: 22.5 percent of residents are 65 or over, and the average household has 2.20 people.

Two thirds of households, 66.4 percent, own their home. That mix of long-time owners and a steady rental market matters if you are selling a house that has been in the family or has had tenants.

Home values, costs and rent

The median value of an owner-occupied home is $352,100. A house with deferred repairs will usually sit below that number, and a fully updated one can sit above it.

Use these as a rough starting point and not as a price for your own house. Condition, lot, and how fast you need to close all move the real number.

Location, schools and commute

Retail defines the city. Rosedale Center and Har Mar Mall are both here, and buyers who work nearby like the short drive. The average trip to work is 20.7 minutes. Interstate 35W and Minnesota Highways 36, 51 (Snelling Avenue) and 280 are the four main routes.

Roseville Area Schools, district 623, serves the city, with Roseville Area Middle School for grades 7 and 8 and Roseville Area High School for grades 9 through 12. Elementary boundaries vary by street, so check with the district for the school that covers your address before you advertise it.

Rental registration in Roseville

If the house is a rental, the city has rules a buyer will ask about. A 2008 ordinance requires owners of rental properties with one to four units to register them every year, and each registration expires 365 days after it is issued. Single-family homes, condominiums, townhomes, twinhomes, duplexes, triplexes and fourplexes are all covered. Short-term rentals are covered too and need a separate license.

  • Post the registration certificate inside the rental unit.
  • A late fee applies to renewals more than 30 days overdue.
  • Renting to relatives is registered without a fee, and so are group homes that hold a state license.
  • Buildings with more than four units, hospital units, hotels, on-campus college housing and owner-occupied homes with unrelated boarders are exempt.

Renewals are done through the city's ePermits site. Before you sell a registered rental, ask Community Development how the registration gets closed out so the new owner starts clean.

Recording a deed with Ramsey County

Real estate documents for the county go through the Recorder and Registrar of Titles Office, 651-266-2050. A recorded document stays on the record for good. If something was recorded wrong, the fix is a corrective document with fresh signatures and acknowledgments plus a correction note.

Ramsey County runs two systems side by side. Torrens land is registered by court order or by the Examiner of Titles and has a certificate of title. Abstract land does not. A document that covers both kinds must be filed with each office separately, either as two sets of originals or by recording one first and then taking the recorded copy to the second office.

  • A transfer deed needs a well disclosure certificate and a $50 fee, or a qualifying statement on the deed.
  • Notary service for real property in the county costs $5 per notarial certificate, and the signer must be present with ID.
  • The office can't give legal advice or blank forms.
  • Liens are released by recording a satisfaction, and both stay on the record.

Property tax due dates and penalties

Ramsey County owners with a tax bill over $100 pay in two parts, ahead of May 16 and October 16. Under Minn. Stat. 279.01, a missed date costs 2 percent on a homestead and 4 percent on other property the next day. The same amount is added again if the balance is still open on the first of the following month, then 1 percent a month through December. Totals top out at 8 percent for homestead and 12 percent otherwise.

The Ramsey County Assessor's Office sets market value as of every January 2 and views each parcel at least once every five years. It also assigns the classification, such as residential homestead or nonhomestead, and the legislature sets a different percentage for each class. A yearly Assessor's Report is posted online.

What a Roseville seller must disclose

Minn. Stat. 513.55 requires the seller to put in writing, before any agreement is signed, the material facts the seller knows that could badly affect an ordinary buyer's use of the house. The statement has to be honest and based on what you actually know, and it can go to the buyer's licensee. Past water in a basement or an addition built without a permit are the kinds of facts to write down.

Do this early, ideally before you list or take an offer. A buyer who sees the disclosure up front has fewer reasons to renegotiate later, and a cash buyer can price the repairs into a straight offer. If you are unsure whether something counts as material, write it down anyway. Ask the buyer's licensee or your own attorney if you want the wording checked.

Steps for a quick Roseville sale

Selling fast is mostly a matter of having paper ready. A rough order that works for most owners:

  1. Pull the current tax statement and see whether the first or second payment is still open, since both dates fall in the same year.
  2. Find out whether the land is Torrens or abstract, because that decides which Ramsey County office handles the deed, or whether both do.
  3. Gather the well disclosure certificate, or plan a qualifying statement on the deed, and bring the $50 fee.
  4. Write down known problems such as water, unpermitted work or past repairs, so the disclosure is ready before an offer arrives.
  5. If a tenant lives there, confirm the rental registration is current and ask the city how to close it after the sale.
  6. Arrange for all signers to be present with ID so the notary can complete the deed at the $5 per certificate rate.

A traditional listing adds showings, a buyer's loan and an appraisal. A cash sale skips those steps, so the timeline depends mostly on title work and how quickly the recording paperwork is ready. Houses with repairs, back taxes, or tenants are the usual fit for a cash buyer, who takes the property as it stands.

Frequently asked questions

Does a Roseville landlord pay a registration fee to rent to a relative?

No. Rental properties where every renter is related to the owner are registered without a fee, and owners no longer need to notarize the exemption affidavit.

How long does a Roseville rental registration last?

It lasts 365 days from the date of issue. The owner renews online through ePermits, and a late fee applies once a renewal is more than 30 days past due.

Which Ramsey County office records my deed?

The Recorder and Registrar of Titles Office, at 651-266-2050. Abstract land goes to the Recorder and Torrens land goes to the Registrar of Titles.

What penalty applies if I miss the May tax payment on a Roseville home?

Two percent of the unpaid amount for a homestead and four percent for other property. More builds up month by month until the legal cap.

Who needs to hand over a written disclosure when a Roseville house sells?

The seller does, before signing, and the paper can go to the buyer's licensee. Minn. Stat. 513.55 is the rule.

Your options for selling in Andover

Owners in Andover have three paths: hire an agent and list, sell the house yourself, or take a cash offer from a buyer who accepts the property as it stands. All three end with a signed purchase agreement and a deed recorded in Anoka County.

One duty follows you down every path. Before you sign to sell a home, Minnesota Statutes 513.55 has you hand over a written disclosure of known material facts that could significantly hurt a typical buyer's enjoyment of the house, stated in good faith. Giving it to the buyer's agent counts as giving it to the buyer.

Before you choose, pull together four items:

  • Your latest Anoka County tax statement and parcel number.
  • Permit records for plumbing, mechanical, roofing, basement or deck work done on the house.
  • The city rental license, if tenants live there.
  • A draft of the written seller disclosure.

A cash offer tends to suit owners who want a short timeline, face repairs, or hold an inherited house or tenants. Get any offer in writing, and make sure the number allows for tax owed and any open permits.

Andover housing market

Andover is a city of about 33,874 people in Anoka County, up 3.9 percent from the 32,601 counted in 2020. It is overwhelmingly owner-occupied, and households run larger than average. Most of Andover belongs to Anoka-Hennepin School District 11, but a narrow northern strip falls under St. Francis Area Schools, District 15, so confirm the address before naming a district to a buyer.

Andover housing figures, 2020 to 2024
Housing measureAndover
Owner-occupied rate94.1%
Median home value$410,200

Persons per household3.00

Median household income is $137,593 in 2024 dollars. Individual streets will vary around these citywide numbers, so ask for recent sales on your own block.

Andover permits to check before you sell

The Building Department warns that work done without a needed permit has to be disclosed at sale and that code violations can delay or devalue a deal. Before listing, check your past projects against the permit list.

  • Permits are required for new construction, remodeling, additions and alterations, basement finishing, decks and porches, roofing, siding, irrigation systems and solid fuel fireplaces.
  • Plumbing permits cover water heaters and water softeners. Mechanical permits cover furnaces, air conditioners, boilers and gas fireplaces. Electrical work needs its own permit.
  • Septic systems need an installation permit and a designer and installer who meet Minnesota Pollution Control Agency rules. Pumping a septic tank takes a $20 permit that the pumper obtains.
  • No permit is needed for detached accessory structures under 200 square feet, sidewalks and patios, painting, flooring, cabinets, or normal maintenance such as replacing deck boards.

Homeowners may pull permits themselves, but a residential contractor is usually the better choice. Residential permits are typically approved right away or within one or two days, and about a third are applied for and paid online. The Building Department is at 1685 Crosstown Blvd NW, reachable at 763-755-8700 or building@andovermn.gov.

If a past project turns out to have no permit, ask the department what it would take to close it out before you list. Fixing that early is cheaper than a buyer's inspector finding it, and a cash buyer will still price the problem into the offer.

Rental houses in Andover

Single family and multifamily rentals both need a city license and inspections. A license lasts two years, each rental gets at least one inspection in that span, and a new owner cannot take over the old license.

That matters when you sell a house with tenants in it. A buyer who plans to keep renting must obtain a fresh license, so mention the tenancy early. The city's rental page links to Chapter 8 of the Andover ordinances and to the Minnesota Attorney General's landlord and tenant information.

Anoka County property taxes when an Andover house sells

Anoka County prints a single statement for each parcel, mailed in mid-March. A deed recorded after January 1 does not prompt a second mailing, so the bill goes to the earlier owner, and a duplicate must be requested. A missing statement is no excuse for a late fee.

Payments are due May 15 and October 15 with no grace period, and a deadline on a weekend rolls to Monday. Online payment goes through PayAnokaCounty, with card payments at 2.6 percent and ACH e-checks at $3.50. Checks go to Property Records and Taxation, 2100 3rd Avenue, Anoka, MN 55303, or to the counter at the Government Center. A free direct payment program is explained at 763-323-5400. For mailed checks the postmark decides timeliness, so ask a post office clerk for a hand-applied one.

To see what a parcel owes, search the county's property information by parcel number or by house number plus the first three characters of the street name, for example 4th rather than 4th Street. If the street shows as unassigned in the tax system, use the parcel number printed on the statement. The Government Center counter in Anoka is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays, and a tax drop box sits beside it.

What happens from offer to closing

Once you accept an offer, the purchase agreement is signed and the written disclosure is already in the buyer's hands. The title company or closing agent then orders the tax figures from Anoka County, checks that no permits are left open, and prepares the deed. Closing is where the tax payoff is deducted and the deed is signed. The deed is then recorded in Anoka County, and the certificate of real estate value goes to the county auditor.

On a cash sale there is no lender appraisal or underwriting step, which is why those sales can finish quickly. The disclosure, permit and tax items do not go away, though, so start with them.

Two steps sellers miss

A homestead owner who sells should report it to the assessor inside 30 days, or the county can strip the homestead and add penalties. At recording, a certificate of real estate value also goes to the county auditor (Minnesota Statutes 272.115). Proposed statements for the next year land in mid-November and become final only after levies are approved in December.

A simple order keeps the closing smooth. Get the written disclosure done first. Then check permits, then the tax balance, and last any rental license. A cash buyer can often close on your schedule, but each of those items still shapes the offer, so having them ready lets you compare bids on equal terms.

Frequently asked questions

How fast can I sell a house in Andover, MN?

It depends on the route. A listed sale waits on showings, financing and inspections, while a cash purchase removes the lender from the timeline. Either way, the written seller disclosure comes before your signature.

Is a permit required to swap a water heater in Andover?

Yes, a plumbing permit covers water heater and water softener replacement. A furnace or air conditioner falls under a separate mechanical permit.

Which school district serves Andover?

Most of Andover is in Anoka-Hennepin School District 11. A small strip along the northern edge belongs to St. Francis Area Schools, District 15.

Who sends the Andover property tax statement?

Anoka County does, each March, and its Property Records and Taxation office takes payment. If nothing arrives by April 1, call 763-323-5400 for a duplicate.

Must I tell the county when I sell my Andover home?

If it was your homestead, yes: report the sale to the assessor within 30 days to avoid lost homestead status and penalties. The county auditor also receives a certificate of real estate value.

Savage at a glance

Savage is a Scott County city facing the Minnesota River from its southern shore, roughly 15 miles from downtown Minneapolis. Water marks the northern edge, and the Credit River flows through town into it. Total land area is 15.61 square miles.

Growth followed the Highway 13 upgrades of the 1980s and the Bloomington Ferry Bridge, which opened in 1996. The city had 26,911 people in 2010 and 32,465 in 2020, with a July 1, 2025 estimate of 32,970. Families dominate: a typical household has 2.74 people, and one resident in four is under 18.

Housing numbers

Owners occupy 85.8 percent of Savage homes, and about 93 percent of residents were in the same house a year earlier. People stay put, so many sales here are family moves, estates, or houses long overdue for updates.

Roads and school districts

Most local traffic uses Highway 13 and County Road 42. I-35W and U.S. 169 run just beyond the city limits. Parts of the Minnesota Valley National Wildlife Refuge and the Murphy-Hanrehan Park Reserve lie within the city, which helps homes near open space.

A house can belong to any of three school districts, a detail that is easy to miss in a listing:

  • Prior Lake-Savage District 719, with Redtail Ridge, Hamilton Ridge and Glendale elementary schools feeding Prior Lake High School.
  • Burnsville-Eagan-Savage District 191, with Harriet Bishop and Hidden Valley elementaries and Eagle Ridge Middle School feeding Burnsville High School.
  • Shakopee District 720.

Buyers will ask, so find out which district covers your address before the house goes on the market.

Rental registration in Savage

Registration is mandatory and free. Savage's residential rental ordinance, Title 11, Chapter 121, requires owners to register so the city and emergency services have a contact for each rental. The city ties the program to Crime Free Residential Rental Property training offered at several Minnesota locations.

If you own a rental and plan to sell, you have three practical moves:

  • Read the ordinance first.
  • Ask the city how to update or end your registration after closing.
  • Pass the registration and training information to the buyer so they can register under their own name.

With a tenant in the house, say early whether the tenant is staying, and keep the registration and training papers in one folder. A buyer who wants to live there needs a different timeline than one who wants to keep renting it. Questions go to the city's property protection pages. Registration is free, so there is no fee to settle at closing, only the paperwork to hand over.

Scott County property taxes and appeals

The fall installment is due October 15. You can pay on eNotices Online, where an e-check carries a $1.50 charge and a card costs 2.3 percent. Mail works too, as do the Government Center drop box and, shortly before a deadline, the box at a county library. Property and Taxation Services is at 952-496-8115.

The Postal Service now stamps the day it first processes an envelope, which may be later than the day you mailed it. Pay electronically, ask a clerk for a hand postmark, or mail several business days early.

Think the value is too high? Start with the city assessor and bring an appraisal or recent comparable sales. Next comes the open book or local board session listed on the value notice, then the county board of appeal. Tax Court is the final stop, with filings due by April 30. Appeals take months, so don't count on one to change the numbers before a quick sale closes.

Scott County Land Records

Scott County's Land Records Department takes in deeds, mortgages, assignments, releases and satisfactions. Call 952-496-8150. Plats and priority documents such as sheriff foreclosures or certificates of redemption need an appointment. Electronic, mail and drop-box recordings are all processed.

  • Property Watch costs nothing and sends the owner an email whenever a document is recorded under their name and parcel number.
  • RecordEASE is the paid portal for searching documents by parcel, by document number, by plat or lien, or by tract index.
  • Staff confirm a document is in recordable form but can't hand out legal forms or advice. They send people to the state's Uniform Conveyancing Blanks, an attorney or a title company.

Sign up for Property Watch before closing so you see the moment the deed is recorded. If a deed or release seems slow, phone the office and ask whether it is still queued or needs an appointment.

Homestead classification and your buyer

Minnesota law links homestead treatment to the certificate of value. Any sale above $3,000 needs one filed with the auditor when the deed is recorded, and without it the property can't be classified as homestead (Minn. Stat. 272.115).

On a sale, the assessor drops the homestead classification for the next assessment year unless the new owner files a homestead application and qualifies. Scott County's Taxation page explains the requirements and takes the application materials. A buyer who forgets the application can face a higher tax bill the following year, which is worth raising during negotiations. If you are selling to a buyer who will live in the house, remind them to file the homestead application promptly after closing. If the buyer plans to rent it out instead, the property taxes will simply follow the other classification, and that is worth knowing before you agree on a price.

What to do first when a Savage house needs to sell quickly

Once you decide to move, these local checks save time.

  1. Look up your parcel number on the county property information site and print the latest tax statement.
  2. Confirm which of the three school districts covers the address.
  3. See whether the city has a rental registration on file for the house and whether any document still needs recording.
  4. Have a title company or attorney prepare the deed on a Uniform Conveyancing Blank, since the county won't.

Then pick a route. Listing with an agent means showings, a buyer's loan and an appraisal, and it fits a house in good shape. Selling for cash skips all three, which leaves title work and recording as the only real schedule drivers. Deferred repairs, a tenant or an estate history don't rule out a quick sale to a buyer who takes the house as is. The parcel records and tax statement you gathered serve either route.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a fee to register a rental in Savage?

No. It is free, though required under Title 11, Chapter 121 of the city code.

Which school district serves my Savage house?

It varies by address, because three districts split the city: Prior Lake-Savage 719, Burnsville-Eagan-Savage 191 and Shakopee 720. Check with them before you advertise.

How can I be told when something is recorded against my Savage house?

Join Scott County's free Property Watch with your name, property ID and email address. You get an alert whenever a document is recorded under your name and parcel number.

Is it too late to appeal my Scott County value?

Minnesota Tax Court is the last step, and its cutoff is April 30 of the payable year. The meetings listed on your value notice come earlier, so read it each spring.

What can't Scott County Land Records help with?

It won't supply legal forms, help fill them out or give legal advice. Staff direct people to an attorney, a title company or the state's Uniform Conveyancing Blanks.

Rosemount housing market

Twenty miles south of Saint Paul, Rosemount marks the southern fringe of the metro in Dakota County. Growth here has been fast. Residents numbered 31,881 at the July 1, 2025 estimate, 24.3 percent above the 2020 base of 25,651. Owners dominate: 87.4 percent of homes are theirs, and 91.5 percent of residents did not move during the prior year.

A typical owner-occupied home is worth $424,100, owners with a mortgage pay $2,266 a month, and owners with no mortgage pay $796. Median gross rent is $1,640 and median household income is $129,625. There are 9,924 households averaging 2.77 people.

U.S. Highway 52, Minnesota Highways 3 and 55, and County Road 42 are four of the main routes, and the average commute is 28.1 minutes, so buyers weigh drive times to Saint Paul, Minneapolis and Dakota County job centers. Independent School District 196, the Rosemount-Apple Valley-Eagan district, serves the city.

A step-by-step order for a quick Rosemount sale

Begin by finding out whether your parcel is abstract or Torrens, since that tells the closing agent what to search. If the house is rented, call City Hall about the rental license and gather the tenant's lease. Write down every material fact you know about the house for the buyer. Look for wells on the lot, since each transfer deed carries a well certificate or a printed well statement. Pick a buyer and agree on a closing date, then ask the closing agent to send the deed, the well disclosure and the certificate of value together. The deed is then recorded in Hastings, and a mailed package returns in a week or two.

What a cash sale skips

Selling for cash removes showings, open houses and any delay while a lender approves the buyer. It does not remove the paperwork. You still give the written disclosure, the deed still needs a well statement, and any sale over $3,000 still needs a certificate of value. What you gain is control over the closing date and freedom from repair requests. What you give up is some of the price an open-market buyer might pay, so set the offer beside what a listing would leave you once repairs, commissions and carrying costs are paid.

Rental license for a Rosemount house

The City Code requires a rental dwelling license under Title 9-8-4, and the housing official may inspect the property under Title 9-8-8. The city's application asks whether the building is a single-family house, a duplex, a townhome or a larger multi-family structure, and whether the license is new or a renewal.

  • An owner who rents out properties in other Minnesota cities must list them on the form.
  • A false statement on the application can lead to suspension or revocation.
  • The application lists a fee of $100 per unit when mailed, so call City Hall at 651-322-2024 for the current amount.

If the buyer is taking over a tenant, ask City Hall what happens to the license. City Hall is at 2875 145th Street West, and the city's website is rosemountmn.gov.

How Dakota County sets values

The road from sales data to a final tax bill takes more than three years. Each year's assessment looks at sales from the twelve months ending September 30 and uses a January 2 market value, which sets the tax payable in the following year. Notices go to every owner in March, and the appeal window runs March through May.

Once the county board adjourns in June, state law bars Assessing Services from changing that year's value. What remains is a Minnesota Tax Court petition, which has an April 30 deadline in the year the tax is payable. The county takes service of petitions at taxpetitions@co.dakota.mn.us or in person in Hastings.

Gather recent sales of similar houses if you plan to question next year's value, and call Assessing Services at 651-438-4200.

What Dakota County needs to record a Rosemount deed

Recording for Dakota County happens at Property Taxation and Records, 1590 Highway 55, Hastings. The office takes deeds at an appointment or through the mail, and a mailed package needs a cover letter, a stamped return envelope and a daytime phone number. Expect the originals back within one to two weeks.

  • The county lists a $46 fee for an abstract document, plus a $5 conservation fee on instruments where deed tax was paid.
  • Card payments for recordings carry a 2.49 percent service charge.
  • A transfer deed must come with a well disclosure certificate, or else carry one of two printed statements about wells.

Most land in Dakota County is abstract property, so the title company searches the records at sale. Torrens property instead has a certificate of title. The county's property search shows which type applies to your parcel. County staff cannot help you complete legal forms, so lean on a closing agent or an attorney.

The certificate of real estate value

Minn. Stat. 272.115 requires a certificate of value for any sale over $3,000. The seller, buyer or an agent files it with the Dakota County auditor as the deed is presented, and it reports financing terms and nets out personal property sold along with the house.

The same section blocks homestead classification in the years after a sale when no certificate was filed, so have your closing agent confirm it is filed along with the deed, and keep a copy for your own records, since it also affects how the buyer's homestead is classified in later years.

Frequently asked questions

Does my Rosemount rental license matter when I sell?

The license applies to operating a rental, so ask City Hall at 651-322-2024 what to do with it when the house changes hands. Rosemount's Title 9-8-4 requires the license, and the housing official can inspect under Title 9-8-8.

Can I appeal after the Dakota County board has adjourned?

Not through the county, because state law bars changes to the value once the board adjourns in June. A Tax Court petition remains possible up to April 30 of the payable year.

Which office records a Rosemount deed?

Dakota County Property Taxation and Records in Hastings records it. Book an appointment, or mail the deed, the fees, a cover letter and a stamped return envelope to 1590 Highway 55.

What is a well disclosure on a Minnesota deed?

Dakota County wants to know about wells on every parcel that changes hands. The deed travels with a completed certificate and fee, or with a printed sentence saying the seller knows of no wells or that nothing has changed since the last certificate.

When do Dakota County property tax statements arrive?

Proposed statements go out in November, final ones in March, and payments are due in May and October.

Selling in Brooklyn Center?

Selling quickly in Brooklyn Center

The quickest sales in Brooklyn Center are those where the owner knows the city's rental, vacancy and utility rules before an offer arrives. Rental licensing and vacant building registration are the two city programs a seller is most likely to meet.

  • An owner-occupied house with no code orders can be listed or sold directly with little city involvement.
  • A rental needs a current city license and a record of its inspection.
  • A vacant house may need to be registered with the city and re-inspected before anyone moves in.

Work out which of the three describes your property, then read the matching section below.

Brooklyn Center housing market

Brooklyn Center is a first-ring suburb in Hennepin County with 31,846 residents, down 5.7 percent from April 2020. Most of its land is single-family homes. For 2020 to 2024 the median owner-occupied home value is $274,300 and 63.6 percent of homes are owner-occupied, so roughly 36 percent are rentals, which is why rental licensing plays such a large role in local real estate. Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage is $1,789, median gross rent is $1,376 and median household income is $72,535. Winter lows can reach minus 25 degrees, so heating, insulation and roof condition are worth documenting for a buyer. Public schools are in Brooklyn Center Schools, ISD 286.

Rental license rules when you sell a rental

You need a license to operate the rental, and the buyer of a rental will ask to see it. Brooklyn Center has required rental licenses since June 1, 1975, and the rule covers any housing that is not owner-occupied, whatever the tax status or whether rent is charged. Short-term rentals such as Airbnb need a rental license too, but an owner-occupied house renting one or more rooms and approved accessory dwelling units do not.

Rental licenses are now issued for two years, and each must pass an inspection that uses city codes, the 2018 International Property Maintenance Code and applicable Minnesota codes. Operating without a license is a misdemeanor and can bring administrative citations and fines. If you are selling a rental, give the buyer the license, the inspection results and the lease files and ask the city whether the buyer must apply for a new license.

Selling a vacant house

Brooklyn Center requires a vacant building registration, and the fees climb the longer the house sits empty.

Residential vacant building fees
Vacant property typeFee
Single-family or townhome, up to one year$595 total ($195 re-occupancy inspection plus $400 registration)
Condo, up to one year$515
Duplex, triplex or fourplex under one owner, up to one year$675, $815 or $950
Any residential type, one to three years$1,000 a year
Any residential type, more than three years$3,000 a year

The registration fee can be reduced by up to $300 if the property has no code violations, but you must call 763-569-3330 and meet the inspector on site before applying. The first year of vacancy needs both the registration and a re-occupancy inspection. Sellers must tell buyers about correction orders, and the buyer can take over responsibility for corrections by contacting the city. The ordinance exists to protect neighborhoods from hazards and blight, and failing to comply is a misdemeanor.

Utility bills and special assessments at sale

Brooklyn Center bills water, sanitary sewer, storm drainage, street lights and recycling quarterly, and it generates a final bill when a property is sold. Final bills are produced several times a month. Delinquent utility bills are certified to property taxes each year as special assessments, with a $50 certification fee added, so a balance you ignore can follow the parcel onto the buyer's tax bill. The minimum residential bill for 2026 is $227.17 a quarter, or $174.43 with the senior sewer rate.

Special assessments for city projects are paid through the Community Development Department at 763-569-3330 before they roll over to county taxes. Ask that office for a payoff figure, and confirm it with your title company before the closing date.

Assessing, taxes and recording

Hennepin County handles all three, not the city. The county assesses the roughly 8,986 parcels in Brooklyn Center, sets estimated market value and classification, reviews each property in person every five years, and takes homestead applications at its assessor's office at 612-348-3046. A new owner has to file for homestead to receive the reduced taxable value, and the application asks for Social Security numbers of owners who live there and the Certificate of Real Estate Value.

Property tax is due May 15 and October 15, and Hennepin accepts payment online, by mail, at the Government Center or by direct payment. Taxes can be included in a mortgage payment through escrow. For recording, Hennepin County Recorder fees are $46 per document, a well disclosure certificate is $54, and an eCRV is required for deeds with taxable consideration over $3,000. Minnesota Statute 513.55 requires you to give a buyer written disclosure of material facts before the agreement is signed.

Steps before you close

Start by confirming which of the three situations applies: owner-occupied, rental or vacant. If it is a rental, collect the license, inspection results and leases. If it is vacant, call 763-569-3330 about registration and the possible $300 reduction. In every case, ask for a final utility bill and a special assessment payoff so nothing rolls onto the buyer's tax bill. Then have the title company confirm the eCRV and the well disclosure items for recording.

A cash buyer who takes the house as it stands can shorten the repair and showing steps, but the city's registration, license and utility rules stay in place. Settling them first keeps the closing date firm.

Two more habits help. Keep every city receipt, inspection result and correction order in one folder, because a buyer or title company may ask for any of them. And call the Community Development Department early rather than the week of closing, since inspections and payoff figures depend on staff schedules. If the house has a long list of open code items, a buyer paying cash may price them in, so a clear written list from the city lets you compare offers fairly. Ask each buyer in writing who will pay any assessment or fee that is still open at closing.

Frequently asked questions

Does Brooklyn Center require an inspection when I sell my home?

Inspections apply to rentals with a license and to vacant buildings, which need a re-occupancy inspection. For an owner-occupied house, call Community Development at 763-569-3330 to confirm whether anything applies to your address.

What does a vacant house cost to register in Brooklyn Center?

A single-family house vacant up to a year costs $595 in total. The fee rises to $1,000 for one to three years and $3,000 beyond three years, and up to $300 can come off the registration with a clean inspection.

Can a buyer take over code violations on a Brooklyn Center house?

Yes. Buyers can assume responsibility for corrections by contacting the city, and sellers must tell buyers about correction orders. A buyer must also meet all city codes and the conditions of the approved property plan.

Is an Airbnb in Brooklyn Center covered by the rental license rule?

Yes. Short-term rental properties must hold a rental license. Renting out a room in an owner-occupied home is the exception.

Who do I call about homestead after I sell?

The Hennepin County Assessor's office at 612-348-3046 processes homestead for Brooklyn Center. The new owner files a homestead application with the Certificate of Real Estate Value, so give them the sale documents promptly.

Fridley housing and who buys it

Fridley is a first-ring suburb at the southern tip of Anoka County, just north of Minneapolis, with 30,829 residents as of July 2025. Most of the city went up between 1950 and 1970, which puts much of the housing squarely in the postwar era. Buyers will ask how old the roof, windows, furnace and sewer line are, so write the dates down before the first showing.

Owners occupy 63.0 percent of units, and the median home value is $302,900, which leaves roughly 37 percent of households renting. Investors and landlords are a regular part of the buyer pool. The city has 11,928 households, median household income is $77,680, median gross rent is $1,326 and the average trip to work takes 22.6 minutes.

Rent of $1,326 set against owner costs of $1,793 a month with a mortgage explains why some owners hold an inherited or outgrown house as a rental before they decide to sell.

City code items to fix before listing

Fridley enforces exterior and yard standards that a buyer's inspector or the city may flag, so walk the property first.

  • Grass and weeds taller than an average of ten inches draw a ten-day notice. If the lawn is not cut, the city mows and bills the owner.
  • Driveways must be paved or hard-surfaced. Gravel is not allowed.
  • Garbage, recycling and compost containers belong behind the front setback. They may sit at the curb only from 5:00 PM the day before collection until 9:00 PM on collection day.
  • Vehicles parked outside need current tabs and must be street operable, and cars cannot park on grass.
  • Fence height is capped at four feet in front and seven feet along the sides and back.

If a violation goes unfixed, the city can hire a contractor and add the cost to the property's taxes, or issue a citation with court fees of at least $300. An owner can appeal in writing to the City Clerk within 14 business days. Clearing open notices before the buyer's walk-through avoids last-minute credits. Photograph the yard, driveway and fence once they pass.

Does a Fridley rental need a city license when it sells?

Yes, anyone buying to rent the house out should plan to apply. The city uses two license subtypes: single family covers one to three units, and multi-family covers four or more. Applications are filed in the CitizenServe portal.

The owner must list a physical address, not a PO box, and an owner who lives more than 50 miles away needs a local contact. The owner shown in the portal comes from Anoka County records, which update every one to two months, so a new owner can upload purchase documents with the application. Rental licensing answers questions at 763-572-3616.

Selling a rental? Bring the current license certificate and any inspection results to the table. A buyer who sees clean paperwork moves faster, and a cash buyer can often close with tenants still in place if the lease is in order.

Stopping and transferring the water account

Tell the Utility Billing Division before closing, either on the Moving In/Out form or by phone at 763-572-3529. Staff need a meter reading on closing day to prepare your final bill, and the account switches to the new owner as of that date.

  • Residential water has a fixed charge of $26.01 per quarter plus tiered volume rates.
  • Sewer is billed on winter-quarter water use, and recycling is $11.60 per quarter for homes.
  • Weekly garbage service comes from a private hauler the city approves, billed apart from the city bill.

Unpaid utility charges can become a lien and go to Anoka County to be collected with next year's property taxes. Notices go out on or before October 1 for balances billed through July 31, and a 10 percent late fee can apply to past-due accounts.

Schools and school districts

Most of Fridley is in Fridley Public Schools, Independent School District 14. Small parts of the city fall in other districts: a northern area is in Anoka-Hennepin District 11, an eastern area is in Columbia Heights District 13, and much of the north-northeast belongs to Spring Lake Park District 16. Confirm the district for your own address before you list.

Buyers also search by commute. Interstate 694 and Minnesota Highways 47 and 65 are the main roads, and the Northstar commuter rail line stops at the Fridley station, which is a useful selling point for anyone working downtown.

Recording a deed and paying tax in Anoka County

Anoka County records Fridley deeds. Tax payments are made at 2100 3rd Avenue in Anoka (Property Records and Taxation) or through PayAnokaCounty online. State law splits the year's tax into two halves due before May 16 and October 16 (Minnesota Statutes 279.01).

Anoka County recording charges for a deed

Paying online adds a 2.6 percent fee for cards and $3.50 for e-checks. Checks and in-person payments at the Government Center carry no fee.

Do I have to disclose problems with my house?

Yes. Ahead of signing a purchase agreement, put in writing every material fact you know that could significantly affect how a buyer uses and enjoys the property (Minnesota Statutes 513.55), and do it in good faith. For a postwar house, think about old plumbing, past basement water, and any additions done without a permit.

Ways to sell and what each involves

An agent listing fits a house in good shape, though showings, inspection requests and loan approval take time. Selling on your own saves the commission and hands you the forms and the haggling. A cash buyer takes the house as is, which helps with code notices, a tenant-occupied rental or an inherited property. Before accepting any offer, ask what the buyer expects you to fix, who pays closing costs and when you must move out. Get the answers in writing, and compare the net amounts rather than the headline prices. If the house has an open code notice, hand the buyer a copy of it and a note on what you have already fixed. That avoids a surprise at the final walk-through and keeps the closing date from moving.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell a Fridley house that has code violations?

Often, yes, but check the notice first. The city can add abatement costs to the property's taxes, and buyers often ask for credits. A cash buyer takes the property as is, while a retail buyer may ask you to fix flagged items first.

Who do I call to close my Fridley water account?

Call the Fridley Utility Billing Division at 763-572-3529 before closing. The city needs a meter reading on the closing date, and that date ends the seller's account and starts the buyer's.

How much is deed tax on a Fridley home sale?

State deed tax is 0.0033 of the net sale price once consideration exceeds $3,000. Anoka County collects it, along with a $5 conservation fee, when the deed is recorded.

Does the buyer of my Fridley rental need a rental license?

Yes, if they will rent it. The city licenses rentals of one to three units and of four or more units, and a new owner applies through CitizenServe. They can upload purchase papers while the county's owner record catches up.

Do I have to disclose problems with my Fridley house?

Yes. Minnesota Statutes 513.55 has you put known material facts in writing, in good faith, before the purchase agreement is signed.

Selling in Oakdale?

Where an Oakdale owner starts when a sale has to close soon

Your options are an agent, a do-it-yourself sale, or a cash deal with a company that buys as is. Cash usually moves fastest, since it avoids showings and buyer financing, and it suits a fixer, a tenant-occupied house, or an inherited place nobody wants to keep up.

Under any option, the deed gets recorded in Washington County, the well question has to be answered in writing, and a rented house needs an Oakdale license. Each point is covered below.

Oakdale housing snapshot

Oakdale is a Saint Paul suburb in Washington County, and it is growing and mostly owner-occupied. The whole city sits in school district ISD 622. Rentals still exist in town, and the city has a licensing program for them.

Oakdale housing at a glance (population is the 2025 estimate, the rest are 2020-2024 averages)
Housing measureOakdale figure
Residents30,588, up 8.1% since April 2020
Homes occupied by owners77.5%
Midpoint home value$318,100
Midpoint owner cost with a mortgage$1,793 per month
Midpoint gross rent$1,481 per month
Midpoint household income$93,772

There are 11,566 households of about 2.45 people each, and 92.5 percent of residents were in the same house one year before.

The Oakdale Dump Superfund site

A buyer who asks will want a straight answer. The Environmental Protection Agency lists the Oakdale Dump at North Hadley Avenue and North Granada Avenue as a Superfund site. It covers three separate properties that served as dumps in the late 1940s and 1950s: a 55-acre site, a 5-acre site and a 2-acre site. Waste disposal there contaminated soil and groundwater with hazardous chemicals.

Cleanup has been carried out, and operation and maintenance work continues. The area was converted into a city park. For a house close to that corner of town, read the EPA site profile before you list, and keep your private well statement accurate if the property has a well.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Oakdale house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Oakdale rental licenses and permits

Every rental needs a city license that covers January 1 through December 31. You apply on the online permitting portal. Staff review it, email you for payment, and book an inspection before issuing the license. The housing standard is the current International Property Maintenance Code.

  • Building permits that need no plan review take three business days, and those needing review take ten.
  • Ask for an inspection five business days before the day you want it.
  • Call 811 at least 48 hours before digging a fence post or planting bed.
  • Most Oakdale lots carry an easement, so sheds, play structures and raised beds should stay out of it.

Permit and license records completed after February 6, 2023 can be searched by address on the online portal. The inspections office at 3200 Granada Avenue North answers questions at 651-739-5150, which helps if a buyer asks whether an older deck or addition was permitted.

Well disclosure when you sell

Before an agreement to sell real property is signed, Minnesota Statutes section 103I.235 obliges the seller to hand the buyer a written statement. The statement either says no wells are known, or it supplies a legal description, the county and a map and says whether each well is in use, not in use or sealed.

  • At the closing, either a well disclosure certificate is filed with the county recorder or the deed itself states there are no wells.
  • A completed certificate costs $54 to record.
  • Individual condominium units are excluded.
  • A buyer who sues within six years can recover sealing costs and reasonable attorney fees from a seller who knew, or should have known, about a well left off the statement.

Skipping the certificate does not undo the deed between the parties, but a county recorder may not record a deed that lacks either the no-wells statement or the certificate. Settle the answer before the closing table, and walk the lot first so you know whether an old well, even a sealed one, needs to be listed.

Recording the deed in Washington County

Washington County records real estate documents at the Government Center, 14949 62nd Street North in Stillwater. Real property records are handled at that building only, while tax payments are accepted at all five service sites, including the Woodbury center at 1261 Woodlane Drive and the Stillwater location. Documents can also be recorded online through state-recognized vendors.

Fees are $46 for a deed or mortgage and $54 for a well certificate, plus a state deed tax of $3.30 per thousand dollars of consideration. At $3,000 or less in consideration, the deed tax is a flat $1.65.

  • Property Watch is a free email alert that tells you when a document is recorded under your name.
  • Racial covenants still found in old deeds can be discharged for free.
  • A tax parcel split needs all taxes paid in full, plus surveys and deeds bearing city approval stamps.

Due dates and penalties on Washington County tax

State law requires half to be paid before May 16 and the rest before October 16. A late first or second half adds a penalty of 2 percent on homestead property or 4 percent on nonhomestead property, with a matching increase the next month and 1 percent more each month through December. The cap is 8 percent for homestead and 12 percent for other property. Any unpaid amount is settled from your proceeds at closing, so pull your tax statement early and look at both halves. A buyer or title company will ask which payments are already made, and a clean answer keeps the closing date from slipping.

What to confirm with a cash buyer

Ask for the terms in writing and check each of these against the Oakdale and Washington County steps above.

  • Who completes the well statement or certificate, and who pays the $54 recording charge?
  • If the house is a registered rental, who finishes the current license year and how is any tenant handled?
  • Whether unpermitted work such as a deck, fence or finished basement will change the price or delay the closing.
  • The amount you receive after the deed tax and any unpaid taxes are paid at closing.

A short written list keeps the closing on schedule, and it gives you a plain way to compare a cash offer with a listing that would take months.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a license before renting out my Oakdale house?

Yes. Oakdale licenses all rental property for a January 1 to December 31 term. You apply on the online permitting portal, pay when the city emails you, and pass an inspection.

How long does Oakdale take to review a building permit?

Three business days when no plan review is needed, and ten when it is. Call 651-739-5150 to check the current turnaround before you schedule closing-related repairs.

What happens if I forget to disclose a well on my property?

You may owe the buyer the cost of sealing it plus reasonable attorney fees, when you knew or had reason to know of the well and the buyer sues within six years. The deed itself stays valid.

How much extra do I pay if my Washington County tax is late?

A homestead payment takes a 2 percent penalty right away and the total is capped at 8 percent, while nonhomestead property starts at 4 percent and is capped at 12 percent. A mailed payment postmarked within one business day of the due date can have the penalty abated once.

Is the Oakdale Dump a reason to avoid buying near Hadley Avenue?

That is for each buyer to decide with the facts in hand. Cleanup has been done, maintenance continues, and the area is now a city park. Share the EPA profile if a buyer asks.

Selling in Chaska?

Selling fast in Chaska

The quickest sale in Chaska goes to a buyer who does not need a lender: an investor or cash buyer who purchases as is. A conventional listing usually brings a higher price but takes longer, and selling without an agent leaves the paperwork to you.

  • Choose a listing if the house shows well and your calendar is flexible.
  • Choose a private sale if you already know who will buy.
  • Choose a cash sale if the house needs repairs, has tenants, or belongs to an estate that has to settle.

Chaska has detached houses, townhomes and duplexes, apartments and condominiums, and homes in manufactured home parks. Each type draws its own buyers, so match the sale route to what you own. A detached house usually does well on the open market, while a park home depends more on park rules and financing.

Chaska housing at a glance

Chaska is the Carver County seat, about 21 miles southwest of Minneapolis, with downtown on the Minnesota River. Main routes are Chaska Boulevard, Pioneer Trail, U.S. Highway 212 and Minnesota Highway 41, and the Highway 212 freeway carries a bus rapid transit route toward the Twin Cities.

The July 2025 population estimate is 30,513, up 9.7% from the 2020 census count. For 2020-2024 the median owner-occupied value is $404,700, the median gross rent is $1,553 a month, and the median household income is $110,956. Owners live in 67.6% of homes. The 2020 count showed 10,788 housing units with 3.2% vacant and a rental vacancy rate of 4.0%.

What kinds of homes Chaska has

Detached single-family houses are the largest share of the housing stock, and townhome and apartment growth since 2010 has been modest. The city's 2040 comprehensive plan tracks the stock by type.

Chaska housing units by type, 2010 and 2017
Housing type20102017
Single-family detached4,9685,700
Single-family attached1,6051,699
Manufactured homes682669
Multi-family2,0352,227
Total9,29010,295

Just over 25% of homes were built before 1980 and about 8% before 1960, while more than 40%, some 4,132 units, went up after 2000. The manufactured homes sit mainly in two parks. The Metropolitan Council counted 68.6% of units owner-occupied and 27.6% rented in 2018.
